THE FREE 4JHITRCHES.
THE BEGINNING OF THE u MAT" MEETINGS.

"May" is really not an adjective of time but -an adjective of quality. The May meetings extend over at least six months. The annual gatherings of the National Free Church Council, which are always held in March, are at the beginning of the series, and the meetings of the Wesleyan Conference, which always run into September, conclude it. An exact enumeration of the anniversaiies, conferences, and assemblies that are held during that period has not, as far as we know, been made, but it is pretty certain that the figure would run into several hundreds.

div.head: NATIONAL FREE CHURCH COUNCIL. •
div.p: THE NATIONAL FREE CHURCH COUNCIL. •

The great annual gatherings of this organi- sation are to be held this year at Bradford from March 10 to March 13. The Bradford 'people are preparing to Offer a true Yorkshire welcome to the thousand and more representa- tives who will attend the sessions. Bradford has had considerable experience in the re- ception and entertainment of great public as- semblies; for the Church Congress, the Wesleyan Conference, the Congregational Union, and the British Association have visited the town. The welcome given to the representatives is no mere matter of receptions and speeches. It means supper. bed, and breakfast to all the representa- tives who are not making private arrangements. The National Council is visiting Bradford at the invitation of the local Free Church Council, one of whose Secretaries is Mr. A. R. Byles, a proprietor of the Yorkshire _Daily Observer, so well known for many years as the Bradford Observer.

div.head: NONCONFORMITY IN BRADFORD.
div.p: NONCONFORMITY IN BRADFORD.

'There are many interesting episodes in the 'history of Nonconformity in Bradford. At the passing of the Act of Uniformity in 1662 several clergymen in Bradford and neighbour- hood resigned their livings. The Friends have been established in the town for two and a half centuries. Their earliest meetings were held at the house of John Wynn, a clothier, who was repeatedly stripped of all he possessed by the ruthless tyranny of the time. The Baptists at first met in a pri- vate house and then in a 'cockpit. The worshippers brought their own stools—or buffets," as they say in Yorkshire—with them, while the pastor eked out his modest stipend by still pursuing his trade as a -weaver. The influence of the renowned J. P. Chown is still felt in the city. John Wesley visited Bradford in 1744, and the Wesleyan Methodists are the most numerous Nonconformist ,commwaify in the town.

div.head: TEE NEW PRESIDENT OF TEE COI7NEIE.
div.p: TEE NEW PRESIDENT OF TEE COI7NEIE.

Rev. W. J. Townsend, D.D., will succeed the Rev. J. G. Greenhough, M.A., as President of -the National Council. Dr. Townsend's address is being anticipated with the keenest interest. He is a distinguished minister of the Methodist New Connexion, and has held the highest offices in the gift of his denomination. Dr. Townsend has worked hard for the Federation movement since the first Free Church Congress was held at Manchester in 1892. At that gathering he read a sensible and excellent paper on "Comity and Co-operation in Mission Work." Dr. Townsend has written a large number of volumes, one of which, a Handbook of Christian Doctrine, has been translated into several languages. During the year of the Cromwell Tercentenary he wroto.an excellent popular life of the Protector.

div.head: DR. PARKER.
div.p: DR. PARKER.

Dr. Parker will be nominated at the Bradford meetings as President for 1903-1904. There is Lot the least doubt that the nomination will be ratified by enthusiastic acclamation. Dr. Parker will be the third Congregationalist who has occupied the Presidential chair of the Council, the other two being the late Dr. Berry and Dr. Mackennal. There is a strong probability that the next member of that de- nomination to receive the honour will be the Rev. J. H. Jowett, MI., but some years must elapse until that day comes. Dr. Parker's scheme for a United Congregational Church does not make much immediate progress. However, there must always be some considerable period betweeu the seed-time and the harvest of a _great idea.

div.head: SERMONS.
div.p: THE SERMONS.

The programme that will be set before the representatives at Bradford contains many in- teresting items. Four sermons are part of the bill of fare. What is known as the Council sermon will be preached by Dr. Robertson Nicoll, of the British Weekly. It is seventeen years since Dr. Nicoll was a minister in charge of a church, nevertheless there is no preacher who, week by week, addresses so large and so influential a congregation as Dr. Nicoll reaches by the leading articles in his journal. His dis- course at Bradford will be heard by an audience representing the flower of the Free Churches in all parts of the country. The other preachers are to be the Rev. J..G.Greenhough, M.A. (who, as retiring President, will preach the opening sermon), the Rev. F. W. Macdonald, and the Rev. C. Silwester Horne, M.A. Thus the four great denominations—Congregational, Baptist, Methodist, and Presbyterian—will be worthily represented.

div.head: FEAST OF FAT THINGS.
div.p: A FEAST OF FAT THINGS.

Indeed, practically all the leading Free Church ministers and many of the most promi- nent.laymen will take part in the proceedings. 'The resolutions on public questions will not include one on the war. The General Com- mittee at a meeting which was attended by representatives of the conflicting bodies of opinion on the South African question unani- mously decided that the matter should be left alone at the Bradford meetings. The attend- ance at the Committee on this occasion was the largest on record.

div.head: SOME OTHER ITEMS.
div.p: SOME OTHER ITEMS.

Discussions on the specific work of the move- Inent of course occupy an important place in the programme. Among the other items is an address on "The Use of Wealth," by Rev. W. P. Hartley, J.P., of Aintree. It is well known Mr. Hartley has for years devoted a certain definite proportion of his income to religious and philan- thropic work. Dr. Clifford will no doubt have something very interesting to say on "The Housing of the Poor."

LADIES' LETTER
MT DEAR NELLIE,

A charming blouse is tight-fitting over a silk Lining, cut away at the neck, a useful and effective theatre or dinner garment. Blouses are still plain and chic in outline, but an infinity of pains is expended on them in the form of tuck a and rib. binge, embroidery and lace insertions and appli- -quis, with fascinating results. The bolero blouse, as it may be called, having a vest within a vest, is well-worn style, but the favourite simple kind, a -soft pouched front set into a lace yoke, has gained too strong a hold upon our affections to be aban- doned lightly. For evening gowns, though it was to be expected that colours would be much in request after such a long abstention from them, all "white or black toilettes seem most worn. White taffetas, white tulle or mousseline, worked A lingerie, make the mast' elegant robes.

• Of au the hats worn during the winter none has excelled in good effect the white beaver or white silk with sable brim and a knot of blue or old rose silk or velvet, with sometimes a bit of good lace draped rather irregularly. But now people are thinking of their new hats for spring, and the new straws are of a very fascinating description. They are all light in weight, though many are rather rough of aspect, while others are silky, and crino- line straw is as light and supple as possible. In some of the newest hats the straw is in half-a- dozen different colours, skilfully combined in a fashion that permits no one colour to be conspicu- ously predominant. A combination of orange, tan, brown, and soft amber is very successful tor early spring wear, not being aggressively light in tone, a mistake that is often made when don- ning a spring hat in company with a wintry-looking costume

A boa or ruffle is hardly likely to be so iniqui- tous this spring as it was last year, still there are some people who never abandon this dressy addition to the toilette, in fashion or out of fashion. It will probably reappear under the guise of the pelerine or tippet, flat in shape and more suited to the exigencies of the Louis XV. and 'XVL and the Empire styles of dress which will prevail than the round kind. A pleasing change from the chiffon and lace ruflls was one worn at one of the great weddings of last week it took the form of a collar with revers above a failing cape collar, of soft brown chiffon. The collar and revers were of rich gold guipure, both edged with sable, and long ends of brown chiffon plisse, caught hi here and there with sable tails. fell to the feet in front.

In hats, flowers are now becoming paramount. A very pretty hat had the crown entirely of the palest blush rose buds, whilst the upturned brim, very wide and deep across the back, was formed of blue forget-me-note, with their green leaves, two pale blue choux at the back taking away any bare look. Another hat, which was a novelty for morning wear, with a tailor gown, was of light crushed strawberry straw, the upturned brim formed of large open rings of the straw, through which was laced foulard spotted with white, tied in a large fringed bow at the back, this being the only trimming. It is not everyone who can wear the flat hat, which is the fashionable order of the lay, therefore many of these plateau hats have an upstanding still brush aigrette in front, a little to one side, an upstanding tuft of flowers, or a wired pouf of tull, simulating an ostrich tip. The plisse or knife-pleated skirt is once again having a great vogue, and it looks particulary well under rich silk coats with lace jabots which now prevail. These skirts have been in fashion on and off since their first introduction many years ago, for they are particularly becoming to slim figures, and adaptable to the thinner materials, such as mousseline and crepe de chine. There are infinite possibilities of good and economical dressing in this skirt, for if of black, in crepe do chine, it may serve as a dressy day costume with a coat of rich brocade, the pattern necessarily having some black in it to accord with the skirt, or it is equally in place with an evening corsage, either a jacket shape or an ordinary décolleté pouched bodice of blaci lace or net, with touches of colour. In selecting the crepe de chine for such a skirt, which is to serve a double purpose, it is well to choose the very best quality, which will not get limp or rusty looking, nor lose its pleat easily. Black and coloured taffetas will be very well worn for dresses in the early spring and later on, trimmed with plenty of lace and many rows and quaint rosettes of ribbon velvet. The proper making of these rosettes is worth a little study, for they appear a good deal on the skirts or new models in varying sizes, and are used instead of buttons on boddices. To make them as buttons ribbon of about half an inch wide should be selected, pleaded up very finely and stitched on to a small centre (a plain fiat linen button will do) round and round in three or four rows, and a strass or turquoise stud set in the middle to finish it.
Your loving JENNIAL

div.head: BY MARGARET WATSON.
div.p: BY MARGARET WATSON.
PART VI.-CONTINUED.
" That's silliness," said Alice's father, " you it promise what you like, but you'd forget all that when you wanted to do summat else, or you'd be the fust 'ooman as didn't."
" Oh, father! I wouldn't forget. I sent Eben away, and now he's married." She choked back a sob.

" Yes, that's very fine. You thinks 'cause he's married you won't want to marry no one else, and that's why you're so spry with your promises. No, my gal, I knows better, and I ain't agoin' to trust to no promises." "Then will you part me from Nelly ?" "I don't see why you should be parted from Nelly," he said rather uneasily. "If that woman walks in I walks out," said Alice, standing up, and moving a little back from her father.
"Well, that's as yon like. It's true it don't want two grown women to do the work in this place. But I ain't said as yet as she be to walk in." Alice made a little movement towards 'him.
" Oh, father !" she began. lie waved her back with his pipe in his hand. "But I don't see neither as you'd be so bad off in service • most gals 'ud be glad to yarn a bit for themselves."

"So might I have been, but it's Nelly, father, it's Consty and Nelly as I've brought up you might say, and I can't think what they'll do without me." "They ain't babies. They'll get along all right." " Well, I can see as you've made u.p, your mind, and nothing won't turn you. But I hope as you'll tell me time enough when it's to be—for when that woman walks in 1 shall walk out."
" I don't say as 'tis to be, Alice." "May I 'ave that box of my mother's as she had when she was in service ?"

"Oh, yes, you may 'ave that." Then Alice left him, and with a slow and weary step climbed the steep stairs to the room she shared with her two little sisters; and that night, and many a night after, she cried herself to sleep. One Sunday morning, about three weeks later, Loveday turned round as he was starting for Church, and put his head in at the door again to say: " There mit be somebody come into tea this after- noon, so mind you has it decent." • .
Alice flushed crimson, but gave no answer, and Loveday waited for none. _

- - As soon as he was gone she snatched up Nelly, and began kissing and crying over her, and Nelly patted her cheeks, :And asked her who'd been naughty to her, and Consty stood close, and fingered her gown and leant up against her, but was silent. She vaguely felt that a terrible misfortune was hang- ing over them all, but she was a quiet self-contained little thing, and looked on and suffered agonies of terror without saying a word about it. Then Alice put Nelly down and told Consty to take care of her while she went across to Mrs. Giff- kens for a minute.

Mrs. Giffkens was busy about her Sunday's din- ner. Alice stood inside the room, which looked cheery with its bright fire and clean Sunday face, and watched the finishing touches given to an apple pudding. "Well, what is it ?" asked Mrs. Giffkens, vig- orously tying the knots in the pudding cloth. " She's comin' in this afternoon," answered Alice. "No ! Is she i'" Mrs. Giffkens hands fell from her pudding. "Yes. Father ;said as how somebody might be comin' in to tea, and I must have it decent.' Alice choked over the words.

"There, child, don't take on—but there, I says that, and I takes on near as had as you do. It do seem 'ard." "I shouldn't care if 'twas someone ari'd be kind to the cluldern, and bring 'em up nice. But to give 'ern up to Sally Limpus ! It do seem as though I can't abide it, and she burst into tell's. Mrs. Giff- ken's eyes filled. "There," she said, wiping them with her apron. "I ha' gone through a good bit in my time, but I do think this seems worser to me nor an, of my own troubles. But tain't no use, us ha got to bear what's sent us. But this ain't like sickness or any- think of that, it do seem as though it didn't ought to be."
"That's jest what makes it so hard, and how to make things nice for that Sally Limpus this after- noon. _lt seems as though I can't."

"I don't wonder at y'ou. But tain't no use say- in'can't ' agenst must.' I knows you ain't got no cake. I made a bit o' dough-cake yesterday. I'll give you 'alf that. It won't do for her to be turnm' up her nose at your 'ouse-keepin'. Is there anythink else ?" "No, thank you. I suppose I must put out mother's best cups and saucers, or father'd be angry, but I'd rather smash 'em and put 'em behind the fire. Fancy his putting a woman like that in our mother's place !" "You manwell say that. However, here's the cake and welcome, and you can send the childern across if you'd like 'em out o' the way at tea-time," and Mrs. Gifikens divided a flat cake, showing a few currants on its white face where it was cut.

"Thank you, Mrs. Giffirens," said Alice. "It do seem a shame to take your cake for that woman— but I'm glad of it. I hadn't a bit of anything extry this week. He might ha' told me yesterday.', So she went back to the children. She got her father's dinner, and they sat down to it together, but tlie meal passed over in almost total silence. Loveday made a few uneasy remarks, but Alice only answered " yes " and " no " and even Nelly was silent and subdued. In the afternoon the tea was set out.

The best tea-things were a pretty fluted pet orna- mented with blue and gold. The cloth was white and whole, though coarse. The black-handled knives had been carefully 'cleaned since dinner, and the cake occupied the post of honour in the centre of the table.

But there only two people set for. Alice had taken an early cup of tea with the children and then sent them across to Mrs. Giftkens ; and she was now standing in the cottage door, looking over the waste December garden, and the bare December trees, as the early dark came on. A click of the gate sent her indeors in a hurry. and. with trembling hands she lit a tallow candle in a tall old iron candlestick, and put It on the table, and infused the tea.

, She heard voices. A flattering, affected woman's and the soft, slow tones cff her father, and in a moment more the two figures darkened the cottage door. The man short and thick set, with a yellow fringe of beard under his chin; the woman rather taller and stoutish, dressed in a smart bead-trimnted mantle, a bonnet with bright yellow roses, and a dark stuff gown. Her comptexion. spoilt with wear and tear, and china-blue eyes were notimproved by a distinctly red nose. Alice stood, tall and slim but iiwkwardly,lvith her hand on the chair at the tea-tray and her eyes fixed on the tea-pot. Sarah Limpus came forward with her hand out " How do you do, Alice ?" she said. " I'm very pleased to see how nice you've got everything." But Alice kept her hand on the chair and did not look up nor speak—only turned very red. Sarah Limpus sniffed.

" Set down, set down," said Loveday, trying to make up for Alice's lack of welcome. "I'm very pleased to see you in my place." "That's more than some other people are I can see," said Sarah tossing her head. " However— I'll take my mantle off if you've no objection, Mr. Loveday—the room's rather warm." " Alice, help her off with her mantle," conunanded her father. Alice did so, and took the mantle and laid it on a, chair. Then they sat down, Alice taking the tray. " Where are the children, Alice f." asked Sarah in her smoothest tones. " I did count on seeing the children."
Alice looked down, and her lips quivered, kit she did not speak. "Alice, don't you 'tar as you be spoken to Where be the childern 2" demanded her Father.

"They're at Mrs. Giffke—n;s, father," answered Alice without looking up. " Oh well, I daresay I shall see them another time," said Sarah, keeping her anger down. "I'm BO fond of children," she went on, addressing herself to Loveday. "Always was—l always liked to be in service where there was children, and they always took to me—they knovv's very well who likes 'em— your Nelly is a sweet pretty child, I must say she does you credit "—turning again to Alice. Buid Alice still sat silent her face on her hand, her black lashes almost resting on her flushed cheeks. " Takc another cup o' tea, do," ,put in Loveday hastily, seeing Sarah's face growing scarlet and her eyes furious An spite of her efforts at self-control. " Alice, fill Miss Limpus's cup up." Alice took the cup which was held out to her, Riled it, and handed it back, without glancing at the obnivacue visas—

" -gold Sarah with a fierce laugh. "I should be afraid to drink it if looks could poisoi. It appears to me as if some folks—namin' no names —have had their ownlway a little too long through 'avin' a good kind Father as didn't like to oppose 'em, and they think now as they can rule over him and make him do what they like and treat a re- pectable woman as has lived in good 'ouses and knows what manners is as if she was the dirt under their feet. But I'd have you to know, miss," sud- denly changing indirect for direct attack, " that you won't be missus 'ere much longer, and then it'll be for me to say whether I'll 'axe you at 'ome for 'olidays and such—and that'll depend entirely on your be'aviour and so I tells you, miss." Alice said nothing but her face was grertving white, and Loveday looked uneasily from one to the other. Sarah swallowed her cup of tea in a few angry gulps and then rose and snatched up her mantle. " I'll be goin' now, Mr. Loveday," she said, "and I hope as you won't ask me to darken your doors again as long as that ill.be'aved gal is within them. For if you was to go down on your bended knees and ask me I should not do it—and I can well see how uncomfortable you must have been with a gal with a obstinate sulky temper like that." She was shaking with anger, and vainly trying to match the hook and latchet at the neck of her mantle while she sought for some taunt that should compel an answer from Alice. But Alice sat per- fectly still and her face was a dull white.

LOveday glanced at her with some compunction. " Never mind her," he said ; " she'll get used to it prensely—she don't like lea yin' the childern. I'll walk 'ome with you," and he got his hat and put a clumsy arm round the woman's waist, "you wants me .to take keer on you, I know."
" You will have i'cui joke," she responded, cover- ing her fury with smiles. ..
'AB they went out of the cottage door together Alice raised her head and looked after them. A look. of utter despair and misery.
CitsrrEa VII.
A few weeks went by, and then one morning Loveday said to Alice : "The lock on that box o' your mother's wants niendire—you mit as well get it done."
Alice toOlc this for her scentence of exile, and closed with the offer of a place as general servant which an aunt of hers, who lived at some distance, had ob- tained for her.
And she was right. The next Sunday the banns wore published. _ _

All.the following fortnight Alice was busy clean- ing the house from top to bottom. So many tears mingled with the water with which the rooms were scrubbed that Mrs. Giffkens felt obliged remonstrate. "Why, child, .if you cries like that it'll be salt water as you scrubs the floors with, and that won't dry out." _ _ _ _ _ _ _

'Alice hardly spoke to her father, and he kept ikostly out of her way, well satisfied that she in- tended to leave the place clean for his new wife. Before the day came (the very Sunday the banns were out) it was finished. Upstairs the boards were as white as hands could make them. The red bricks of the living room were freshly reddened—the plates stood in shining rows on the dresser. The old elbow chair was polished till you could see your face in it. Sarah Limpus had been staying with a married cousin about ten miles away, for the last month, and the wedding was to take place from her house. Mrs. Thornton was truly thankful to be rid of Sarah —so said the housemaid—but Sarah herself told har- rowing tales of Mrs. Thornton's sorrow at parting with "a servant she could thoroughly trust." Loveday walked over to the bride's residence in the morning and they were to be driven home at night. Alice was to find a corner for that night in Mrs. Gitrken's crowded house, the next morning she was , to go to her situation. She took the two children to church on the Sun- lay morning, and choked over the singing of " A few more years shall roll," wishing almost that she snd the children together were with the mother " at rest."

As they went up from church one and another spoke to her. Every one was sorry for the girl who ;Lad filled a mother's place to the children and must mw leave them. s' But she scarcely answered them. 3he could not, and hurried home. The neighbours gathered in little groups and dis- xuised the question for the hundredth time. "There," said Mrs. Giffkens, with tears in her yes, " It's jest the same with Alice as 'twould be to ne if I'd got to go away this night and, leave my thildren to a strange woman." "I'd a'most rather bury 'em first, I should know then as they was took care on," said, a mild-voiced, White-faced woman.

"I never thinks as you ought to fret so over-much when you lose one on 'em," remarked an old woman, with dark, pathetic eyes, "for you never knows when TOU may he took yourself, and then they may be gin ;o anybody to look after, I ha' sin it many's the rime."

" I can't think why the men aint got, more sense," said Mrs. Giffkens impatiently, " anybody could ha' told that man how she'll turn out. He'll wish Alice back again in three months, or my names not Mary Giffkens. Men ain't got no sense, that's what I ray." One or two men had joined the groups and Listened approvingly but this was going too far : " One on 'em had sense enough to choose you seemily, Mrs Giffkens, so we ain't all fools," ze- marked a little dark man, with quick eyes. A low laugh went round the group. "Ain't much choosing, as I see, when you're young, it's mostly chance then," retorted Mrs. Giffkens, "and it do seem as though chance was better nor choosing, for when man comes to choose round he do mostly make a fool of himself and take whatever woman'll wheedle him into it. It's my belief as Loveday was on the look-out ever since the time Eben Clack wanted Alice, and as soon as ever Sally Limpws said 'please' he said thankye.' 'Cause he was after a woman as'd saved a bit. He'll find himself mistook there' that I do know," "Mummy, I wants my dinner," said a small child dragging at Mrs. Giffken'e hand. And the group dispersed. It was a cold day and came on to snow in the afternoon, increasing towards night. Alice spent the rest of it alone with the children. Sitting over the fire with Nelly in her arms all the afternoon, exhort- ing them to be good children' and telling Consty that she must be a little mother to Nelly now. She could hardly bear to put tha child out of her arms while she got the tea, and took her up again, when it was ready, to share her plate and cup. After tea she bathed them both. This was not generally done on Sunday night, but Alice knew she would not be there to do it on Monday morning. She lengthened out the operation, in front of the fire, rubbing softly the firm round limbs, and kissing / the dimpled feet over and over, eS Nelly lay in her lap, warm and soft, and put them up to be dried. And then for the last time for long enough Consty knelt at Alice's knee in her white nightdress, and Nelly knelt upon her lap, with her little arms round her neck, and they repeated their prayers together. And when Alice added, in abroken voice "Pray God keep Welly and Candy when Alice is gone, and take care of them, and make them good girls." Nelly broke out in passionate sobs, realizing the closeness of the parting, and Consty cried too, more quietly, but the little body quivered and shook as she hid her face on Alice's knee.
Alice sobbed with them, for a time, but soon she checked herself and them :
"Hush Nelly dear, Nelly don't erY and Aliee'll sing to her, Consty dear, don't. I must get Nelly to sleep. It wouldn't do for you to be cryin', when they gets home."

Consty ceased almost at. once. Nelly cried more quietly all through the first hymn, and by the time the second one was half over the heavy eyelids dropped over the dark-blue eyes, and Nelly was asleep though stirring, and catching her breath, sobbingly, at in- tervals. Alice pang on, hymn after hymn, till the sobs ceased, and the breathing was even awl regular. Then, for her own comfort, she sang throue.. "Abide with me," and Consty, sitting wide awake, leaning against her knee and staring into the red embers of the are, gather° I, half unconsciously, some comfort be.

"In life, in death, Oh Lord, Abide with me," Alice ceased singing, but Nelly did not stir. So she rose quietly and carried her upstairs, Consty pattering barefoot behind, and tucked them both into the bed she had, till now, shared with them. Then she kissed them. Nelly, lightly, lingeringly, unwilling to disturb her, loath to leave her her so, Consty,iFarraly and often, until _the heard a sound of wheels on the road :

" There they are, I must go Consty," she whis- pered, unloosing the little clinging &rms. and with one last kiss she left them. She had just time to make up the fire, and set her chair back against the wall, leaving all straight, and then as she opened tho door he heard their voices, her father's and his new wife's, saying goodnight and thanks to their driver. s She closed the door behind her and fled across the garden in the darkness, through the softly-falling 511419.

The King and Queen will be accompanied by ' the I Prince and Princess of Wales, on their visit to Devon- port and Plymouth next month for the launching of the battleship Queen. Their Majesties who will be the guests of Lord Mount Edgecombe will proceed and return by special train,but the yacht Victoria and Albert will be moored at Davenport, and the King and Queen will entertain a numerous party On Board the Royal yacht on the 7th of March. On the following day Queen Alf xandra will perform the ceremcny of launching the new battleship. Great preparations are being made at Plymouth in honour of the Royal visit, which will be one of special interest to the Prince of Wales. The Britannia which be entered as a boy in 1878 is stationed at Devonport, and Admiral Lord Charles Scott, the Commander-in-Chief at Plymouth, was Captain of the " Bacchante " when that veesel: made its memorable voyage with the two young Princes on beard. ' Mies Charlotte Knollys, who has scarcely yet recovered from her long and serious illness, has been staying with the Duke and Duchess of Fife at Brighton. The Queen thought that this change would benefit her old and con- fidential friend, and Mks Knollys is just as much a favourite with the Queen's daughters am with her Majesty. She was appointed lady-in-waiting shortly after the Queen became Princess of Wales in 1863, and since than Miss Knollys has rarely been away from the Royal circle at Sandringham and .Marlborough Rouse.

ihe new Marchienes;of Dufferin makes another addi- tion to the list of American ladle' who have become peeresses. She was a Miss Flora Davies, of New York. and had a fortune of her on n when she married the present Mai quis about Bor 9 years ago. Th.- successor to Lord Dufferin is his Second Non, the Earl of Ava haying been mortally wounded in the last attack made by the Boers at Ladysmith. The Marquis has three Fitters. The eldest Lady Helen. is married to Mr Munro Ferguson. Tho second, Lady Hermione, is a 'hurse by profession and training, and the third, Lady Victoria, is the wife of Lord Planket. Much sympathy is felt for the widowed Marchioness, who was the greatest help to Lord Dufferia during his long and distinguished diplo- matic career. She is a moat clt.yPr and accomplished woman, and has written several books on her experi- ences in foreign countries, among others" Our Viceregal Life in India," and "My Canadian Journal." . . . . . .. . . . _

Such is the British. in-stinct for business that many people in London are insuring against the rirk of con- tracting smallpsx. More than one of the large assurance companies are issuing policies at the rate of 23 61 per £lOO. io the event of one taking smallpox within six months. This rate is for the recently vaccinated, a higher premium being required for the unveceinated, and no doubt separate policies will soon be issued covering the risk of any evil affects arising from being vaccinated. Fen tunately. few smallpox policies will be issued for more than £l,OOO, as even for this sum, it is conceivable that there are many persons who would deliberately contract the disease, and take their chance. Nothing is more important to the woman of limited means than a careful and trained judgment in matters of dress. There are some women who always present a smait appearance,even upon the most slender resources, whilst there are others who are always buying new clothes and yet never have anything to wear. One of the Secrets of an economical toilette is to have what few gowns one can afford well made, in a plain but becoming style, strictly avoiding those little fads of fashion which are here to-day and gone tn-morrow. Another important point is to adhere to the colour that is most complimentaryito one's appearance, end make that the keynote of one's whole scheme of dress. Theme are the two golden rules for an economical wardrobe, and the Test is .11 a matter for personal care. There is an art in putting clothes on, as well as in taking them off, and they shou:d never be laid away unbrushed, nor should we omit to " tree" all boots and shoes when taken off. Glovea too, waz t care- ful attention, and one should never sit in a walkisg dress indoors.

The Princess of Wales made a few purchases of enamel jewellery at the Society of Women Artists Exhibition the other day. There were some beautiful specimens of artistic jewellery on view, and one of the purchases made by Fier Royal Highness was a necklet composed of tiny beads in blue cloiseort.; enamel, with pearls intro- duced between each on a slender gold chain. Another purchase of the Princess's was a set of blue and white enamel buttons. These artistic buttons are very beau- tiful, though scarcely so much worn now. Leading the lingers with rings and jewels, and the wrists with bracelets are the particular forms which extravagance in jewellery seems likely to take this year. ehe effect of the fancy sleeves, nhich are appearing in many of the newest black, white, or cream silk or chiffon bodices, is extremely good. These sleeves ale usually built of insertion laces one heavy and one light the latter possessing two or three rows of holes through which tó ribbons are drawn. To the renovator, the idea will be a welceme one. Many among us possess bodices which would prove of the greatest use, but for tbe sleeves which date them. The new fancy sleeves may be quickly and very inexpensively fashioned, also a transparent yoke to march, which is a neeessity unless a little of the insertion lace appears as a trimming upon the bodice.

With the soft pale brown costumes so modish at the moment, brown veils spotted with black have appeared. To the wry few do they prove becoming, but they are "correct," and so numbers of smart women are wearing them. The recent severe weather has driven many who had given up veils, to take to them again, but the wise will restrict their choice to the plaio, clear black nets, which boast neither spot or pattern. There is no doubt that. r )wded thoroughfar a the baby carriage is a good deal in the way on the pave- -12106t,. This is particularly noticeable outside those shops which attract the attention of nursemaids, and invariably bring them to a standstill. It is this want of movement, rather than any tendency to travel at a terrific pace, that causes the trouble, and it is therefore Ii tie difficult to understand the necessity for the new eider, adopted by the Kent County Council, that every ! perambulator or mail cart, being a vehicle, must .Jarry a ' light after dark. Such a regulation scarcely seems to be needed in the public interest, UV; in Kent it behoves the nursemaid' and others to beware lest they are caught by the vigilant policemen without a light or lantrra of some sort if out with the baby carriage after dark. 'The observance of St Valentine's Day, which used to be quite general, seems to have fallen almost entirely into desuetude, Why it used to be observed was never quite clear, for the origin of its recognition seams to be involved in as much mystery as the authorship of the poems whie,h we know as Homer's. One writer gives a list of fifty-two St Valentines,and there were two wboqe death is commemorated on February 14th. Dr Brewer attempts an eaolanation,but only adds to the unc2rtain- tv when he decl tree that Valentine is a corruption of the French word galantin, a toau. 'The list of Spring novels which have been, and are to be published by the house of Methuen and Co., is a very interesting and inviting cue. To mention a few of tbe books, " The Story of Teresa " (A Macdonnell) has already apeeired, also, " The autocrats " (C H Lush), " Drift " (L T Meade), and Edith Reckests " Out of the Cypress Swamp," while toward* the and of the month we are promised yet another book from the pen of Mies Adelaine Sergeant, viz., " Tee Master of Beach- wood." "The Victors " by Hobert Barr, and several other works. In March we are to have " Those Delight ful Americans" by S J Duncan, and in April " Love , grown Cold," by Amnia Swan. MADGE.

div.head: OBLE
div.p: OBLE
Creditable Performance by Warring- ton Squads._

Warrington teams were highly successful at the annual competition in connection with the St John Amhulance,or"first-sid" work,by men employed on the Cheshire Lines Railway which was held yesterday week in the station buildings, Rauslagh-street, Liverpool. .Mr David Meldrum (general manager) presided, and among the large attendance were Messrs R Marlton, H T Heathcote (Brunswick), J Leather, C Adkins, W Howes, J W Ruches, S Deming. J C Ellison, G Mason, T Pratt, Dr R Smith, and J W Bird. The arrangements were carried cut by Mr E 0 Lloyd, boa secretary, and In every respect the competition proved a great success. , Eight squads entered for the contest, as follow : Liverpool Central, Brunswick Goods Station, Buskisson Goods Station, Warrington Central Station, Warring- ton Stores Department, Warrington Engineers' Depart- ment, Manchester Central Station, and Birkenhead (Shore-road). Each squad consisted of five men, whilst Dr Fde B Pins officiated as judge. The tests, which were not known to the Men before they entered the room, were of an interesting nature. Tile contest resulted as follows :-1, Warringtan Central Station (II T Williams, J Fogg, H Holloway, H T Roberts and 4 r Robertson) ; 2, Warrington Engineers (W Newts, .1 Newns, J Tomlinson, J Lee, and T Downie) ; 3, War- rington Stores Department (G Grease., 111 Wellfare, E (1 Hughes, H Clements, and G Grozier). At the conclu- sion of the distribution of prizes, performed by lairs Meldrum, the chairman proposed a hearty vote of thanks to Mr Lloyd for the great amount of interest be took in the competitions. This was seconded by Mr Everitt and carried. A vote of thanks to the chairman for presiding terminated the proceedings.

div.head: CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIPS.
div.p: CROSS-COUNTRY CHAMPIONSHIPS.
Sankey Harriers Performance at Haydock.

The annual cross-country championships meeting took place at Haydock Park on Saturday For the Northern Counties Senior Championship, 12 clubs were entered. The race was keen and exciting, Salford finishing six men in the first 18. and winning with an aggregate of 59 points against Crewe (the holders) 82. Had Morris run up to form, however, Crewe would have probably repeated last year's victory, Leeds were a good third and Farnworth, though having three men in the first ten, finished fourth. The Junior Championship was decided, over a course some three miles shorter than that over which the Seniors ran. All the 25 clubs which had entered sent teams, most of ttem running the full complement of cornpeti tore. The Juniors bad to run three laps, and cover the plough once. The winner, G Butterfield, bad the race in hand all the way, and won as he liked from F W Webber (Sutton), and T Devliu, of Sankey, the latter of whom was second last year. Butterfield was a complete outsider, but he is a fine runner, and being ably backed up by his fellow members, the Darlington club had the satisfaction of not making their lone journey in vain, for they won easily with a total of 83 points. Sutton Harriers were a respectable second, the third place being secured by Sankey Harriers with 213 points. Details :

1 JUVENILE'wgZIO/CEEL9. —A. Bill to restrict smoking by children was read a third time in the House of Keys. Isle of Man, on Tuesday. The Bill as sent up to the Legislative Council renders children under fourreer, years of age liable t 3 fine and imprisonment for smok- ing, and dealers liable to similar punishment for selling ciearettes to children under the age named. The sale of tobacco in other forms to them is not forbidden. Judge Ridley. sitting in the Criminal Court at New- castle, on Tuesday afternoon, complained of insufficient light and fined the conrtkeeper £lO. I James Wilson, the elderly roan who, after being com- mitted to penal servitude for five years on Saturday by Mr Justice Bucknill at the Liverpool Assizes, attempted to cut his thro.t on leaving the dock. is progressing towards recovery. The wound which he inflicted was never very sericw, but it had the effect of getting his sentence reduced from five to two years.

div.head: MAN WHO NEVER LOOKED
div.p: THE MAN WHO NEVER LOOKED
BACK.

Hatton Football Captain's Hint Worth Taking. As most rcaders of this journal are aware, Hatton, in Cheshire is one of the quietest little villars in the whole of United Kingdom. The nearest railway Ptatlon is two or three miles away, and from January to December the inhabitants lead • very peaceful and un- eventful life. There is, however, one event in the year which always creates considerable local interest and enthusiasm, and that is the annual show in connection with the Horticultural Society. Numerous prizes are offered for distribution amongst the auccessful com- petitors..

Several of these were carried off last year by Mr. George Leach. This gentleman's brother, Mr. William Walker Leach, lives at Ivy Cottage, Hatton, and, although only twenty-seven years of age, has had a remarkable history. He is a man of many parts, but is probably best known as the captain of the" Hatton Villa" football tsarn. Be is a fine well-built young man, and has fcr some years been an ardent disciple of Izaak Walton,and hasalso carried off prizes as an athlete, but about twelve months ago symptoms of sciatica pre- sented themselves, and ultimately he became quite incapacitated and. had t? give up his work as a gardener, until he was happily resitored to it, and to health thanks to Dr. Williams' pink Ptlls for pale pelple. Hs had pre- viously had naedi calatenrion for some time.

(From a photograph by Sixties, Warrington.) " Interviewed by a reporter of the " Warrington Guardian" the other day and asked to Id! the story of his cure in his own words," be willingly did so. "1 had," he said, " to give up my favourite football, and I could not follow my employment. I had to stay in the house, and at times was in great pain. I could not sleep, and when I awrke in the morning I was terribly troubled grith vomiting. It did not matter what food I had; it mide no diffi r,nce. I was also troubled with bleeding trom the nose."
" But," interposed the preasman, " you look all right now. What has brought about this wonderful change? You are cne of the moat vigorous looking men I ever saw."

'• I saw an article in the" Warrington Guardian,"and snother in • The 'Christian Herald,' relating to the wonderful cures which had been effected by taking Dr Williams' pink pills for pale people,and I resolved to get a box, which was purchased in London."

. " How !erg, were Dr Williams' pink pills taken before you noticed an improvement 2" " After the first box there was a marked improve- ment. I could eat better, and I felt better. Mv ' tone' was better all round. I could not at one time wallt without limping, and I can say that Dr William? pink pills have done me incr3 gnod than any medicine I ever had. I can say that truly." "sow many boxes have you taken altogether 2" was the next question._

" I have taken five, and I have never had sciatica since. They have done me a world of good." "And you have infinite faith in them ? " Yee I have great faith in them ; I always had. A box will set me up at an time." " Where do you get Dr Williams' pink pills from ?" " From Boots, the chemist, in Bridge-street, Warring- ton." "And what is the state of your health now ?" _ .

" I have had goad health ever since— f-co-rnmeaced taking Dr Williams' pink pills, and I have recommended them to my people." " Dave you any objecticia to the particulars of your case being made known to the public 2" asked the journalist. . _

"Not the slightest" came the unbesitatiag reply. "and I do so for the benefit of the public." Farther questioned by the reporter, Mr Leach said he had beta playing at football quite recently, and that be intended to walk to Warrington—a distance of three or four miles—on the following Tuesday or Wednesday on businets. He had not " looked back" since he commenced to take Dr Williams' pink pills for pals people. He ascribed his cure entirely to them. and emphatezed the remark that be bacl "every faith "in them and " wou,cl never be without them." ThiA interview with the reporter took place in the presence of Mr W W Leach' a mother and several of his younger brothers and eisters, all of whom cor- roborated his statement. His father is very well known in the district, and occupies the post of school attend- ance and inquiry officer for the Daresbury United District School Board. The family are old residents and Watityans, and they, as well as the son, who granted the" Knight of the Peri " this abort Interview, are firm believers in the wonderful efficacy of Dr Williams' pink pills for pale people. -

It shows Mr Leach t i be, as he indeed is, in a vigorous state of health, and there is little probability that he will ever be troubled again with a complaint which at one time caused him pain and great anxiety as to the future.

div.head: ANGLO-JAPANESE ALLIANCE: OUR NEW ALLY AND THE BRITISH AND JAPANESE STATESMEN WHO MADE THE AGREEMENT.
div.p: THE ANGLO-JAPANESE ALLIANCE: OUR NEW ALLY AND THE BRITISH AND JAPANESE STATESMEN WHO MADE THE AGREEMENT.

During the last ten days the one subject under discussion everywhere has been the Anglo- Japanese treaty which came as such a political thunderclap even to the best informed, and the debates on the subject have been numerous. Of course, it is a great departure from precedent on the part of Great Britain; but, at the same time, it is not a question of s'acrificing our. "splendid isolation" half so much as would have been entailed by a Continental alliance on the same lines. What is more, Japan is a most virile powe‘c with all the necessary qualifications for a desirable ally, while in the East, as well as more generally all over the world, our interests are identical. Again, the treaty promises to prove a great impetus to trade' and is, therefore, acceptable in the main to all the other Powers, even Russia. America has expressed its cordial approval, while France and Germany seem not unfavourably inclined on the subject, and are evidently much impressed by the coup. The Muscovites, with their tongues in their cheeks and hankering after Manchuria, declare that its object is simply a principle that they have always advocated—the integrity of the Chinese Empire. This is the most important point of Eastern policy Which is guaranteed by the new alliance, which Cannot but help to act as a check on Russian scheming, which is generally accepted as a fact, despite their smooth denials. Undoubtedly the object of the treaty was to put a spoke in their wheel, as their interests and those of Japan—to say nothing of our own—are totally opposite, at least in Korea and Manchuria. At home the general verdict has been one of satisfaction, although the one fear has been expressed that the Japanese jingoes, who are a power in their land, may be more inclined to spring at the throat of the bear than ever, feeling that they must be backed by us, tacitly at any rate. However, the Government". has, as far as possible, safeguarded the British position in the matter, so that a Russo-Japanese war does not necessarily mean the embroilment of Britain, which would only be brought about if a second Power took active participation against Japan. . The Japs themselves teem wild with delight over the new treaty, and are very pleased with their Ministers. The bulk of the negotions have, of course, fallen upon Lord Lansdowne at home, advised by the Marquis of Salisbury, Sir Claude Macdonald, who left China to represent us in Japan after the siege of the Legations in Pekin, where he was in supreme command, and Baron Hayashi, the Japanese Am- bassador in London. The Mikado himself has naturally taken the keenest interest in its con- summation, as has His Majesty King Edward, while the Marquis Ito, though possibly not directly con- cerned in the actual negotiations, has been leading up to it for years by his general progressive policy. These are the principals who must share the.credit of the new alliance—or the blame, if it turns out a fiasco

regular service—another step in the right dine- tion. Four ships of an entirely new class to be called " scouts " are to be laid down this year, and the armament of some of the battle- ships and cruisers is to be increased, while private yards are to be used for repairs. Destroyers are to be strengthened, and certain new depositions of ships are to be made both on the home and foreign stations, while during the coming financial year the number of ships in the Navy will be notably increased. Lord Selborne's programme is a very economical and inclusive one, and should meet with commendation on both sides of the House in the main. The Army Estimates
THE NAVY ESTIMATES LORD SELBORNE, FIRM
LORD OF THE ADMIRALTY.

show a decrease of over £23.000,000 on those of last year, allowing for a permanent decrease of thirty thousand men on active service, and calculating to maintain some 420,000 men in the field in South Africa for eight or. nine months• of the coming 'financial twelve. In the case of China provision has been made for the retention of a reduced force for about half, the financial year, and the cost of transport back to India—this forecast admitting of a decrease of two millions. It is to be hoped that everything will fall out in accordance with these anticipations, and the nation will gladly welcome the abatement of taxation in these hard times.

One of the well-known features of London, which is doomed to go, or rather to change its character, is Niagara, the celebrated skating-rink. The fat has gone forth, and after March 22nd the regime will be a new one, as it has been purchased by Mr. Paris Singer, the head of the Electric Carriage Company, which supplied her Majesty with her motor-victoria, which she is fond of driving herself in the neighbourhood of Sandring- ham. The present skating-rink will be turned into an immense garage and show-room for these vehicles, which are now quite familiar sights and sounds (with their bells) in town. The demand for them recently has developed the business so grea`tly that the company has grown out of its premises in Denman Street, and Mr. Paris Singer pitched upon Niagara as a suitable site. Last week,- on the eve of its disruption, it reached its apotheosis as a rink, being visited by the King and Queen, the Prince and Princess of Wales, the Princesses Charles of Denmark and Victoria of Wales, and many other notable people, who went to see the figure-skating championship. For it were entered Salchow, of Stockholm; Gordan, of Berlin; Torrome, of the United States and the Figure Skating Club; and Mrs. E. Syers, of the Figure Skating Club, and as may be imagined from the entries a very brilliant exhibition was wit- nessed. Salchow repeated his victory of last year, carrying off the championship, and scoring 365 points. His figures were marvellously rapid and well defined, and as far as could be judged he only made one fault, omitting a loop in a para- graph, but this he amply atoned for when it came to the skating as each pleased. Sir Courteney Ilbert, who has just been ap- pointed Chief Clerk of the House of Commons in the room of the late Sir. Archibald Milman, whose death occurred last week, has a very wide knowledge of legislative methods and forms, as he showed in his work on the subject published last year. He is sixty-one years of age, and was called to the Bar by Lincoln's Inn in 1869. From 1879 to 1882 Sir Courtenay wp, s counsel to the Education De- par tm e nt, but was then nomi- nated to be legal member of the Viceroy's Council in India, under Lord Ripon's Government. It was in this con- nection that his name became for a time familiar as a household word throughout the Empire, being identified with the fierce contro-
SIR COIIRTENAY ILBERT, K.C.5.1., C.1.E.,
'THE NEW CHIEF CLERK OF THE ROESE OF COMMONS.
THE AMATEUR CHAMPION FIGURE SEATER.

versy which arose on the so-called Ilbert Bill. On returning to Eng- land in 1886 he was appointed to the permanent office of Assigtant-Parliamentary Counsel to the Treasury, and „ upon the retirement of Sir Henry JenkYns, -11• C D., he became Parliamentary Counsel to the same Department. The Clerk of the House of Commons is the chief officer of the House who is not a member. He is appointed by the Crown for life by letters Patent, and his official title is "Under Clerk of the Parliaments, to attend upon the Commons." According to Sir Thomas Erskine May, who long held the post, "he .signs the addresses, votes of thanks, orders of the House, endorses the bills sent or returned to the Lords, and reads whatever is required to be read in the House. He has the custody of all records or other documents, and is responsible for the conduct of the business of the House in the official Aepartments under his control. He also assists the Speaker, and advises members in regard to questions of order and the proceedings of the House." He is, in fact, the right-hand man of the Speaker, and virtually the ruling authority of the House. The position, as may be inferred, is a very onerous one, and the duties are yearly becoming more arduous, so that, though to many a man of talent whose labours are not over generously rewarded, a Fti pend of forty pounds a week with an exCellent :house attached may seem handsome remuneration, yet the hire is not disproportionate to the high value .of the services rendered.

Once more we are in the throes of the financial ,year, as, in anticipation of the Budget, the Navy and Army Estimates have been issued during the inst few days. The former is a document of more Ilan ordinary interest, and Lord Selborne's demand for .C 31,255,000 is only a slight increase on the £30,315,000 of a year ago, the difference being 4:1S0,000. 'However, with this the First Lord of the Admiralty proposes to make several new and useful departures. while the personnel of the Navy is to be increased from 118,625 men and boys to 122,7,00. He announces that the recommendations of the Rations Committee are to be adopted, al- • though unfortunately they cannot be got into work- ing order till 1903, by which a standing national 'scandal will be done away with, and he promises a committee (under the presidency of Sir Edward Grey, UP.) to go into the question of reserves, which have not kept pace with the growth of the

div.head: Worthily Supported by Warrington People.
div.p: Worthily Supported by Warrington People.

The hearts of Warrington people have been touched with feelings of profound sympathy by the singularly sad fate which befel a youth named Joseph Marsh a 'NW months ago. Marsh, who is only nineteen years ef age,and upon wh JILL a family of six mainly depend for support, had the misfor- tune to meet with an accident at Bank Quay Station which inflicted such shocking injuries that for a time his ' life was despaired of. At length, the assiduous care end • attention which he received at the Warrington Infirmary had the effect of bringing about his recovery. He is now however, placed in the unhappy position of having to face life a cripple, as the amputation of both his legs was rendered absolutely aecessary to ensure his recovery. It is to be 'regretted that Marsh was not entitled to any compensation whatever from his employers and has therefore been compelled to appeal tothe public for the means wherewith 'to start life afresh. Cause for gratiflation is afforded by the fact that assistance from his fellow work- ingmen in a time of trouble has been speedily forth- coming. A concert was arranged, and most of the tasks involved in its organiz ition were undertaken by members at the working class. A. committee was formed the Rev Fadoer Gibbons being elected chairman, Messrs George Johnson,and W C Brooks,hon.:secretaries,and Mr D.Bate, hon. treasurer, and their efforts were &Glow- ' ably Seconded by numerous sympathisers with the un- fortunate youth. The duty of disposing of the tickets 11 was readily disch•rged by workingmen who devoted their leisure beurs to helping on the good Cause in this way, and, it ia pleasing to know that ; tangible support from the general public was not lacking. The concert took place in the Parr Hall on Saturday evening and the complete success wits which it was attended mast have gladdened the heart of all who assisted in its promotion. The spacious hullo- ing was completely filled, every seat, including those at the rear of the platform being occupied.' An interesting , and 'varied programme had be,sn arranged, and toe manner In which the items were presented gained the ! eordial appreciation of the audience. All honour is due te the local artistes who came forward and ! gave their services to the furtheranes Of such a deserving charity. An orchestra under the conductorship of Mr P Walsh, opened the enter- tainment with the overture " FigarG " (Mozart)! The selection was rendered with marked slaty, due attention being given to expression, and the perform, r 3 were rewarded with unstinted applause. During the evening the orchestra contributed two more selections in praiseworthy style. Quite an array of vocalists appeared and their efforts afforded much pleasure to the audience. The palm must be awarded to the Orpheus Quartet-et (Messrs F Scattergood, J L Davenp ut, E Whitehouse, and L Auklsnd) wh acq.ntt3i tnemselves batter than we have ever heard them b4ore. The voices of these gentlemen blended in such a way as to produce a splendid effect, and their interpretation of "Banks of Allan Water.,' could scarcely be improved upon. In responding to a well-merited encore they conducted their hearers from grave to day, giving a simple narra- tion of Simple Simen's adventure tette the pisaian, and the audience while being moved to hearty laughter by the huthour of the piece were not slow to recognise its musical merits. At a later stage in the proceedings the party sang the pathetic " Massa'a in the cold ground," and the vocal banjo and humming accompaniment were introduced in the most pleasing style. An encore was accorded and In complyingwith the demand ." for more" tho party sang "Annie Laurie." The other vocalists were Miss Rigby, and Mrs W 0 Brooks (sopranos), Mist( H Armstrong (contralto), Mr War- burton, Mr W C Brooks, and Mr J M Bate (tenors) all of whom sang Very creditably. Mr Jfd Bate's interpreta- tion of" Alice where art thou" sod Miss Armstrong's rendition of' A dolly and a coach were perhaps the most acceptable, One of the most enjoyable features of the ctincert was the violin eolo by Mr m Krugrr, who displayed a complete mastery of the 'instrument by his clever performances of "Bemuse " (Fame) and "Mazurka" (Lyzzycki.) Mr E Balmford played the 'cello solos "Dreaming " and "Tarantella" (Squire) in a skilful manner and was very warmly applauded. A duet for the clarinette and flute " Lo! bear the gentle lark" by Messrs W gipkiss and W Ray, with orchestral accompaniments, proved a very pleasing item. Mr J S Pierce provided the humour of the evening and was eminently successful in his effdrta to amuse. His songs " Uncle Jeff" and " To-morrow " were particularly good and created a great deal cf mirth. The duties of accompanist were ably discharged by Mr P Caldwell. During an interval Father Gibbons thanked all who had in any way contributed to the success of the concert and said the spirit in which the whole affair had been taken up was an evident proof of the good feeling that existed among' the working classes. Fellow workmen had lent willing hands for the good cause, and bad shown a spirited determination to make it a success. hey had dol(, the work with a thoroughness that was the glory 01 Euglisis workmanship. It was said things made in Germany were seldom up to our English stand - ard ; and he thought the English standard ot charitable support—judging from the present case—would:ocarcely find its equal. div.head: LONDON EDITOR'S VISITOR.
div.p: A LONDON EDITOR'S VISITOR.

Not long ago the editor of a Landon newspa per wa seated in his private room, intently writing, when suddenly the door burst open and there strode in a bright-eyed,ruddy-complexioned individual,who saluted him with:a violent clap on the shoulders. The editor winced, and looked up with surprise, and recognising a friend, composed his features to a smile. " You are brisk this morning," said the editor, when be had recovered his breath ; " how did you manage to pass my Argus at the end of the passage " Came along tco quick for him," said the intruder. The matter which the g ntleman with the hurricane manner had come about was soon trans toted, and he bad his hand on the door knob ready to depart when the editor stopped him by inquiring how business was. " A.l ," said the intruder ; " everything just as it should be, onl more no. Can't find anything to grumble about. So long !" and, having said these words, he banged the door and disappeared down the stairs. "Ab !" sighed the editor, as soon as his visitor was gone, "that fellow don't suffer from indigestion, I know." The editor was right. Briskness and cheerfulness are not characteristics of sufferers from indigeit.on. Thou- sands of people know this, among them Mr S Kemp, of 19, Roman-road, Chelmsford, Essex. Mr Kemp thus wr:tes, under date 16th October, 1901 : " About eight years ago my digestion got out of order. It came on very gradually—at first with a tightness in the chest after taking feod, followed, later on, by giddiness, faintness, and trembling. I seen became unfit for work, and lost many a day in consequence. To these troubles were seen added palpitation ot the heart, so that I became quite incapable of exertion. For three months I regularly attended the Cnelmsfard Infirmary as an out-patient. At times the medicines prescribed seemed to do a little good ; butin the end, finding my- self no better, I gave up going." Mr Kemp did not know what Course to take next when a little incident happened which we will leave him to relate in his own words. " I met," says Mr Kemp, " with a pamphlet wilich contained particulars of several cases similar t ray own which had been cured by Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup. I was induced to try a bottle. Fram the first my recovery was never in doubt. The pain after meals became gradually less acute, and I felt batter and brighter. I continued to take Mother Seigel'a Curative Syrup for nearly four months, by which time the distressing symptoms dc- scrite I had vanished. Since then I have never been without a bottle of Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup, and by taking an occasional dose after dinner I enjoy excel- lent health, not having lost half-an-hour through sick- ness far the past five years."

BAND OF HOPE ENTERTAINMENI.—In connection with the Hill Cliffs and Stockton Heath United Bend of Hope an interesting entertainment was given on Monday even- ing in Providence Old Chapel, which has been converted into a echoolrcom. The programme consisted of a service of sang entit el " Daisy's Influence." which was given by the members of Mid-street Band of Hope Choir There was a good attendance. The chair was occupied by the President, Rev J 8 Hughes, who extended a hearty 'welcome to the Bold-street friends and also to Nurse Whitfield, of Warrington, who gave the connective readings in a manner which added very much to tho interest of the story. The choir rendered all the musical items most efficiently the various solos, duets, quartettes, Sz c., being Laken by the following members who acquitted themselves very creditably : Mrs Prince, Miss Osborne, Miss Wilson, Mr F Berry, Mr Unsworth, and Mr T Hatch. The service was much appreciated, and reflected credit upon the organist and conductor,Mrs H B H Sander, who ably presided at the harmonium. Op the proposition of the President, a heal ty vote of thanks was accorded to the choir and also t 3 Miss Whitfield for their services, and the singing of the Doxology brought s ye ry pleasant Evening to a close.

NEURALGIA AND WEAKNESS CURED.

Miss L3-diate, of No. 11, jlollins street, Stalybridge, was seen by al Oldham "Standard." reporter, to whom she gave an account of her breakdown in health. "I am forty-four years of age," she added, " and have always been exceptionally healthy," she explained. 'But, about two years ago, I first began to feel very ill. I thought it was all due to indiges- tion. I had a pain in my chest, my eyesight became bad, and I always felt worse after I had had some- thing to eat. I suffered terribly with neuralgia," continued Miss Lychate ; "and I eventually went into the public institution for advice and treatment. " "Did you improve while in that institution? " inquired the reporter. "Well," she replied, "I must say I felt better at the time, but I was still troubled with Weakness, and after I came out I had violent attacks of indigestion. I felt weak and done up." "But you seem well enough now," suggested the reporter. "Yes," Miss Lydiate readily. replied, "I am almost as well as ever I was, and it is owinz to taking Dr. Williams' Pink Pills. I read in the Ashton" Reporter "of a similar case to my own, in which a woman had been benefited by takino. rr. Williams' Pink Pills, so I determined to give them a trial. I took the pills after each meal. After .I had been them regularly for about a fortnight I felt completely cured. The pain in_my chest disappeared. I now feel better than I have done for mahy a day, and I only take the pills occasionally" "You follow your work without suffering any inconvenience ?" questioned the reporter. "I go out working two days a week, and it never seems to trouble me. I have a box of pills un finished, but it is seldom that I neod to take any."

Concert in Buckley-street School.

In connection with "The Girls' Guild," a concert which had been arranged by Mr a Simpson was given in Buckley-street Sohoolromn, the other even- ing, some of the lady workers taking part in it. Miss Bessie Dutton with her usual grace and pleas- antness presided. After the opening hyrnua and prayer, she made a few well chosen remszks, and later she aroused lively interest by one of her read- ings. The audience very much appreciated two songs from Miss GJrnall and one from Miss Ethel Roberts. Miss Fearnley sang " The Holy City," for which she was applauded, and later she gave " Killarney." ''Sc-use that are Brightest " was sweetly sung by Miss Pollie Price, and " Love, the Pedlar," by Mrs Simpson. Miss Sumner also gave a pleasing song. The baritone for the evening was sir Llewellyn Pearce, whe gave two acceptable songs. The Misses Parkinson contributed a piano- forte duet," Qui Vive," in grand style, and were encored. Miss Lizzie Morris and Miss Nellie }Bison recited, and Miss Beatrice Band had to respond to an encere. Mrs Woolley gave pleasure by reciting " Warrington Market," and " Those Happy Days." The humorist was Mr Robert Sumner, ion, who evoked roars of laughter, and on his second appear- ance was encored again and again. Mr Albert Trow ably accompanied,
A Returned Volunteer and His Debts.

At the Warrington County Cou—rt. on 'l7h—u.;:day, before tie Honour, Judge Bowen Rowlands, KA), an action was heard in which Mni Haviour, provi- sion dealer, claimed £4 43 13 from Patrick Roger- son for ' goods supplied.—Nlr Browne represented tie plaintiff and Mr Steel defended.—The case for the phintiff was that goods were supplied on credit to defendant who was the main support of his father and mother, his father being a pensioner in receipt of 5s a week from a railway company. When the defendant went out to South Africa with the Volunteer contingent there was a balance owing of £4 odd. Shortly before his departure,the defendant went to the plaintiff's shot) and in the presence of Mrs liaviour and her daughter Edith promised that he would pay the balance owing. The defendant returned from South Africa last July but he had not paid anything towards the debt and had since got married.—The defence was that the defendant had regularly contributed to the main- tenance of the house and had not authorised the debt in his name. He denied that he had eyer promised to pay the debt. He remembered going into the shop, but when questioned by bis Honour as to what the conversation was about, he said it was only with reference to the weather.—His Honour declined to believe this story and gave judgment tor the plaintiff with costa.:

The Late Sir Herbert Croft. Sir Herbert Craft the inspector of constabulary for the Noithern Division of England, who has 1119 G diel at Lugwardine Court, Hereford, was the representative of one of our oldest county and Parliamentary families. He represented Hereford from 186 S to 1874,and either Hereford or the county had been represented by a Croft in sixteen Parlia- ments from the 3 ear 1293 to the year in which Sir Herbert ceased to represent his native town, In the year 1765 the family most unfortunately had to dispose of Croft Castle, the old sent in Hereford— shire, which had been their's in direct descent front father to son for over seven and a half centuries_ The late baronet, whose title dates from 1671, must net be confounded with the baronetcy won by Sir Jobzi Frederick Croft's predecessors in 1818 for risking his life to obtain information necessary to the,Doke of Wellington in the Peninsular War, and who subsequently distributed £lOO,OOO granted by the British Parliament for the relief of the Portu- guese. His ancestor,who claimed descent from the Crofts of Croft Castle,was knighted by King Charles the First for entertaining his Majesty " toe a sumptious repast at ye house oi ye worthies Kuighte."

Change in the St. Helens Volunteer Camp. For the past sixteen or seventeen years the t3G Helens Volunteer Battalion has gone into camp for their annual training doling Whit weekend several years the weather has proved exceedingly trying. A change has now been brouglt abaur in conse- quence of the transfer of the ha:tenon from the Lancashire Brigade to the South Lancashire Brigade which consists of three of the King's Liverpool Regiments, inCluding the Liverpool Scottish and the Ist South Laucashire,Warrington. August week has been found a great deal more convenient for the majority of the corps, and the St Helens battalion have, consequently agreed. The place for the camp has not yet been fixed, but Salisbury Plain is likely,with Conway as the alternative. The change from May to August should result in the battalion going into camp in an even more co n.— lete and efficient state than usual.

div.head: PEACE AT ANY PRICE.
div.p: PEACE AT ANY PRICE.

"Pace with honour has become a byword. We shall be happy indeed if we can still secure peace at any price. As for honour, we must say with Shakespeare— But all the honour Salisbury bath wan Is that he was a Lord Ambassador." —Bradford, October let, 1885. " LOYALISM."

"Those self-ityled loyalists, who with fulsome pro- fessions of their duty to the Crown . . . . . Preah the law themselves while they put nd to defend R."— Newcastle, January 15th, 1884. THE IRISH QUESTION. . .

"There remains a question . . . and that is to give, in Mr Gladstone s own words, the widest possible self-government to Ireland which is consistent wlth the maintenance of the integrity of the Empire. While we have to conciliate the national sentiment of Ireland, we have to find a safe mean between separation on the one hand . . . and on the other band that excessive centralisation . . . . which stifles the national life."—Birmingham, Jun. 4,11. 1885. TORYI-M.

"This is a very pleasant awl flattering reflection for me to think that the Tory Goverment only ezists to carry out my behests. . . . After a debate the other nights member of the Efousslegf Commons came up to me and said: 'My dear fellow. rray be careful what you ray, for if you were to epeak disrespectfulld of the Ten Commandment• I believe that Balfour would bring in a Bill and reveal them.' . . . . There is. I con- . . .

_ fees, one drawback to the satisfaction that I 'feel. I confess that I shrink from these new allies. . I say frankly that I do not like to win with such instru- ments as these."—Hecknev. July 24th. 1885. TORY CONSISTENCY. .

"We cannot tZvis-at—iiii;r-O--Xicl Change our opinions and put forward new ones every moon an the Tories do. A merciful Providence fashioned them hollow On purpose that they might their principles swallow." Octobei 25th, 1E54. So far the extracts made by the" Liberal Magazine," They are eminently readable, and we add a few more from the many passages that invite quotation : THE '" TIMES."

" I agree with the late Mr Cobden, who said that the opposition of the 'Times' was an indispensable condi- tion of any successful prosecution of Liberal reform."— Glasgow, September 15th, 1885. "DISCORDANT VOICES."

"I do not think there are any of us who will be tempted to desert our own cause and our own party in order to make a new alliance with that heterogeneous combination which styles itself the Constitutional party, and which inclades within its ranks Free Traders and Protectionist, Ulster Orangemen and Erglish Roman Catholics, licensed victuallers and established Church- men.,Tory democrats and fossil reactioniate, all uniting their ditroordatit voices in order to form a mutual pro- tection society for assuring to each of its members place and privilege and rower.—Warrington, September Bth, 1885. THE PEOPLE'S CAUSE. " We cannot trust the t o'ution of these questions to the forced consent of the Tory party, to be refused as long as possible, to be conceded with reluctance, to be granted only when further resistance has become dan- gerous and impossible. The authority, the influence, and the votes of the people should go out at the neat election to the party and to the candidates who have never wavered in their allegiance to the people's cause." —Hackney, July 24th, 1895. THE LAND QUESTION.

- "Land used to be neld In common. Every man who was barn into a community had .his apportioned share in the great natural inheritance of the race, and if he was willing to work his livelihood was assured. Now all that has changed. The birthright of the English people has been bartered away for a mess of pottage, and it has become the possession of private owners of property. I asked the other day what ransom wit prc- perty pay for the natural riehts which have ceased to be recognised."—lPswich. January 14%, 1885. LORD SALISBURY'S CLASS. "I say that in this matter, as in so many others,Lord Salisbury constitutes himself the spelqsroan of a class-7 of the class to which be himself belongs—' who toil not, neither do they spin'—whose fortunes, as in this case, have originated in grants male long ago, for such ser- vices as courtiers render kings—and have since grown and increased while their owners slept, by the levy of an unearned share on all that other men have date by toil and labour to add to the general wealth and prosperity Of the country of which they form a put."—Swanses, February Ist, 1883. THE BOERS.

"The Boers are not naturally a warlike flie,?. They are a homely, industrious, but somewhat rude and un- civilised nation of farmers, living on the produce of the soil. Tbeg are animated by • deep end even stern religious sentiment; and they inherit from their ances- tors—the men who won the independence. of Holland from the oppressive rule of Phillip 11, of Spain—they inherit from them their unconquerable love of freedom and of liberty. Are nct these qualities which commrnd themselves to men of the English race P Are they not virtues which we are proud to believe form the best characteristics of the English people. It is against suoh a nation that we are to be called upon to exercise the dread arbitrament of arms."—Birmingham, June 7tb, 1881. . _
