People who are determined Lord Rosebery's to regard Lord ROSEBERY Speech. as a political pyrotechnist will be disappointed with his speech at Liverpool, In turn of phrase and tilt of epigram it was much less brilliant than the Chesterfield utterance, but in several particulars it was equally important. In the first r it leaveslno doubt as to the ex- Premier's return to public life. At Chesterfield he placed his services at th a command of the nation. At Liverpool he made it clear that he regards himself as re-enlisted among the political workers who mould opinion in and out of Parliament. Secondly, the speech was noteworthy for the can- dour with/which Lord ROSEBERY declared his views. Thirdly, it left no sort of doubt that Lord ROSE- EERY cherishes no illusion as to the formation of a new party to be made by a coalition of Liberal Unionists and Liberal Imperialists. The quid- nuncs who have prophesied a Rosebery- Chamberlain Ministry should at last abandon that idea, which has been unwelcome equally to Lord ROSEBERY and Mr. CHAMBERLAIN. It should be observed that in regard to the war Lord ROSE- BEY adheres to his opinion that Mr. KRUGER and those with him in Holland should not belightly ignored in any peace negotiations ; and he even goes so far as to hint that in his be lief no harm was likely to have accrued from allowing the peace delegates to go to South Africa, as desired by the Dutch PREMIER. The application every- one agrees will be more simple and regular if it be made by the delegates themselves, and it is pretty clear that if they crave the permission Lord ROSE- BERY will criticise the Government if the request be not granted. On the Home Rule question Lord ROSEBERY was very: explicit but not very wise. In throw- ing ever Home Rule he has enlarged the breach between himself and Sir HENRY CAMPBELL. BANNERMAN—a breach which was hardly noticeable and apparently closing. Staunch Liberals and earnest Gladstonian followers cannot reconcile themselves to a proposal which !calmly 'relegates to the limbo of obscurity a pledge once given, merely because at the present time it may be inex- pedient to attempt its fulfilment. The Liberal party must put principle before popularity, and we regret that Lord ROSEBERY should have taken a course which suggests that he prefers the reverse action. Home Rule may not now be in the region of practical politics, but it still remains a sound and seasoned plank in the Liberal platform, and not one to be lightly thrown aside. The Libera leader's re-affirmation on Wednesday evening of his fidelity to the old cause will give great satisfaction to the large body of Liberals who deprecate Lord ROSEBERY'S cavalier treatment of the Irish ques., tion and were so desperatbly disappointed in their expectations by his Liverpool oration. Lord ROSEBERY also spoke in emphatic condern nation of the speeches of Nationalists as to the war in South Africa. There is certainly a great deal of Celtic effervescence about these oratorical out- pourings. Lord ROSE BERY contrasted the valour of the Irish soldiers in South Africa with the virul- ence of Irish politicians in Ireland, Those Irish soldiers who fought so magnificently in Natal were almost Home Rulers to a man, and if they had votes in Ireland would cast them in favour of the exuberant Irish politicians who side with the Boers. That is the paradox of the Irish character. That the speeches of Irish M.P.'s during the war have been deplorable we readily concede. We ook on them as a sign and symptom of that dis- ,sonance between England and Ireland which it ought to be the aim of statesmen to remove.
lace
Three important matters Government's Sins have been under the consideration of Parlia- ment this week, and they may well be grouped together in illustration of the danger of govern"'

ment by a large majority indifferent to public opinion. Fortunately, in the most glaring case, Mr. BALFOUR'S own followers showed a disposition to revolt, and he had to yield to the evidences, to their feeling, and relent. The Cabinet has during the recess been engaged in the task of arranging ' new procedure rules, and it is said that Mr. BAI, YOUR especially has taken a great deal of time and trouble over them. Be that as it may, his penalty clause for contumacy has excited much criticism, and he was compelled this week to pre- sent it recast with the confession that the original form presented unforeseen difficulties. Neverthe less, he had the audacity to expect the House of Commons to accept the change as finally disposing of the matter, just as anyone would settle a little affair of painting or bricklaying,iu a single sitting. The attitude was scarcely courteous to the House, and, happily, he was made to understand this by eing compelled to grant an adjournment. In the other affairs there was a revelation o of the same tendency on the part of Ministers to treat Parliament with indifference by evasion of facts. It is difficult to imagine what harm could have accrued if Lord SELBORNE, when he announ- ced a change of policy in regard to Wei-Hai-Wei, had been frank enough to acknowledge that the alteration was due to a variety of circumstances, and that, in truth, we were no longer under the necessity of fortifying Wei-Hai-Wei. Instead of doing so he gave the impression last week that naval experts had been pondering this subject exhaustively, and had come to the conclusion that the place was useless strategetically. He did not say so, but that was the idea left on the minds of those who heard him. Since then such expert opinion as could be gathered into the newspapers has gone the other way ; and eventually Mr ARNOLD-FORSTER, under pressure by Mr BRYCE, acknowledged that he could not produce any written reports by experts to support the view that Wei•Hai-Wei was indefensible or of no value strategetically. The fact is, of course, that the Treaty with Japan has made the occupation un- necessary. Lord SELBORNE'S explanation was & piece of bluff unworthy of him.

The third incident, hardly less important, was the disclosure that Mr. BBODRICK'S evasion as to the remount inquiry had been studied. Lord LANSDOWNE admitted, under pressure by Lord NORTHBROOK, that General TRUMAN'S demand for a court of inquiry had been forced upon that officer. The events which led to its insistence occurred last August. If Mr. BRODRICK had acknowledged this in the first instance, and been candid with the House,there would have been less suspicion, and something might have been said if he had frankly stated that in consideration for the GENERAL, whose case is "sub judice," the House r must permit him to maint am n an attitude of re- serve. The great majority of members would assuredly have supported him. But Parliament does not like to be played with. This new method of concealment causes distrust, and it tends to supplementary interrogation to an extent which otherwise would not be thought of. The Govern- ment is so confident of its strength in numbers that it is disinclined to take either House into I confidence or to make an appeal to the good sense of the assemblies not to pursue a matter unduly. The remedy for this disingenuousness is to strengthen the hands of the Opposition. An amurath succeeds an amurath. The present Minis- try is so confident of the ascendancy of the Cecil family, aided by the Birmingham influence,that it regards the desire of the House of Commons to share in the responsibilities of government as all ambition to be checked.

Congregationalism in the latter half of the nineteenth century owed much to theßev Newmali Hall, whose death, full of years and honour, occ.irred on Tuesday. There had been bright intellectual stars in its ministry long before his and he had peers—the names of Thomas Clayton, of Ralegh, of Binney, and of Allon spring to the mind; but these were all men of rare natural talent, and Nonconformists were inclined to place , faith, fervour, and gift of speech before scholar ship. Their Puritanism also made them some' what indifferent to the evidences of culture ia, places of worship. As pew-holders grew rich, aria furnished their own homes in comfort and luxury, they were still content to meet on SundaYa in barn-like structures, and often to lief!r sermons which, however excellent for their spirituality, were sadly deficient in ordinal knowledge. Dr Newman Hall was one ?I' the men who did much to change thle, state of things. Bachelor of Arts, Bachelor o,li Laws, Doctor of Divinity, artist, mountaineer av world-wide traveller, he opened his mind to tile light of revelation as few ministers of his 60 did, and by his learning and devotion he was able to shew himself in an imminent degree "a ser vent approved." Those who sat "under him," as the Do senting phrase goes, never had to apologi.s' for him in respect of faulty reasoning, floricleesa of style, or lack of virility. He was a greal preacher, possessing both the intellectual ata" emotional qualities; and by the training whic% be gave himself he reached his eminence—a worknO who needed not to be ashamed. Further thee that, he insisted that Dissenting chapels should as worthy of religion as the well-adorned homes e` the people who attended them. Christ Churel!,' in Westminster Bridge-road, is a monument to b 1; memory: its pulpit of alabaster a tribute 0` affection for his ministry.

The financial position of Japi must be a great factor in determining the yid' of the new alliance, and the point is the more teresting as there have been decided rumours ' ' the rapid development of the country havn I strained its resources almost to their limit. article in question, however, gives quite tine& view of the situation. Before the consolidation , the Empire in 1868, there existed in ti lislands several hundred feudal princes enjoYil absolute power over the provinces, and from the ' comes down an indebtedness which is called t` old loan. Since that date there have been ni°. borrowings' but most for the purposes of rom ways, and of other industries which should sooo' or later prove remunerative. More t11,.,6 £10,000,000 of debt has been paid off, and the ,(P` sent indebtedness stands at about £.;52,000,1Ns It should be noted, however, that of late Joel has been able to obtain money at much In,„°l favourable rates than formerly; and, so far as payment of interest is concerned, an additio; £20,000,000 would impose no greater burden t„.1.1.t £10,000,000 would have done five years ago. 11 a population of 44,000,000, with imports 11,, exports increasing, with wine, spirits, and toln very lightly taxed, and silk, tea, beer, and 11/ other articles not taxed at all, the Finance Seco tary's contention that Japan could, if needed, b,o, a still heavier debt appears to be fairly establis''

On .their Australian form -only Maclaren, Hayward, Barnes, if he recovers, and Lilley will be sure of a place in the English team at home, although Jessop, Bround, Quaife and Tyldesley will be competitors, with anj it- sinhji, Fry, Mason, Jackson, Rhodes, and Hirst for the remaining seven places. With an English tea al selected from these fourteen, England ought to win, and it would have bettor pleased most of us to have had three matches arranged that should be fought to a finish than the plan settled by which there are to be five matches, with the strong probability that unless the wicket is ruined by rain they will be drawn.

div.head: MATTERS OF MOMENT.
div.p: MATTERS OF MOMENT.
A Provincial Letter.

Not just yet are we to have local option in con- nection with the closing of shops. Lord Avebury's Bill, submitted to the House ot Lords on Tuesday, is no new measure. It had already been discussed in Parliament and in the press, and had commanded an appreciable volume of public opinion. Indeei, on two occasions the measure had, without opposi- tion, passed through the House of Commons. But the House of Lords could not this week bring itself to decide that the compulsory closing of shops by a two-thirds local majority would be generally equitable, and so the proposal was rejected on the motion for second reading by a majority of thirty- one votes. It was pointed oat that there were in tr,e measure fairly efficient safe- guards against the infliction of injustice on the individual; but even so, there exists a pre- judice against the compulsory limitation by Parlia- ment of the hours of labour of full-grown men, for the bill proposed to bring under its operation shop assistants of both sexes and all ages. Freedom of contract and freedom of service are held to be the deAderata of citizenship, and those who do not favour the bill as described, but are quite agreeable that the shop as,ist ant as well as the small shop- keeper shall enjoy a more cheerful and less exucting existence Ulm is sometimes the case, maintain that these cenditions can be best secured by volun- tary effort, and not, by the imposition and hard and fast, legislative limitations. It is quite-possible that under the proposed bill the shopkeeper would be prejudically affected.

That the treatment meted out to inmates of work- houses, as a rule, is not of a description which would justify the reluctance of the poor to avail themselves of such shelter as they afford, is clearly demonstrated by It writer in a contemporary periodical, who tells of a Lancashire workhouse in connection with which there was a bowling-green, where four meals a day were give to the children, and margarine was unknown. The writer adds, moreover, that this is not a particularly exceptional institution, inmates of most urban workhouses being treated in the same liberal manner. Be this as it may, and there is no reason to doubt the state- ment& it is a matter of common observation in certain unions that, with improved dietary, the pauper inmate of workhouses is becoming more fastidious. Many stories, culled from the weekly newspaper reports, could be quoted in support. and illustration of this conclusion if space permitted. all of which tend to show what a remarkable change has come over beadledom and the Workhouse system since Charles Dickens wrote "Oliver Twist." It i often sentiment, pure and simple, that prompts the feeling of repugnance manifested towards even modern institutions provided by the money of the ratepayers for the maintenance of those who are no longer able to maintain themselves; and the choice of crime in preference to the workhouse indicates a standard of morals that cannot be regarded as capable of "holding water " or be tolerated any longer. Sympathy is indeed wasted upon the indi- vidual who commits thet tin preference to accept- incr, an offer of the " house." The defence is 'not so effective with country magistrates as it was once upon a time, the prisoner nowadays being very property reminded in such cases that excellent institutions are in reality provided for the destitute who care at the same time ta be honest.

This is the season for kitchen boiler explosions, and Bath has just given us a startling reminder of the fact. An agitation which was started several years ago was believed to have resulted in some good, but the accident alluded to serves to prove that there still exists a certain degree of careless- ness in regard to an abiding source of danger during frosty weather. !Protection against this lurking peril may be established easily and inexpensively ; all that the householder has to do being to fit up the kitchen boiler with a small safety-valve, so that should the water become frozen, during the night the pressure in the boiler would be at once re-, lieved. The expedient of keeping the fire alight is often resorted to, and is efficacious, but it is like- wise costly during a long season of hard frost. It would be absurd, certainly, to urge that there should be any compulsion applied either to the householder to the landlord (why not say house- lord?) to ensure provision of the necessary safety- valve; but the plea of expediency and real danger should suffice to bring about the abandonment of that apathy which has been responsible in the kitchen for so many deplorable and. distressing 'accidents. lathe Bath case this week, the wife of a City Councillor lost her life. It may be added that, if the kitchen boiler be not fitted with a valve, extreme care should be observed t 3 ascertain that the whter in the pipes flows freely before the fire is lighted. Otherwise the risk of an explosion is always great.

" We are on the eve of a mechanical revolution such as has never been seen since the introduction of steam," says the " Times," and the announce- ment appears in large and leaded type. Having read the article that follows the reader must admit that the unusual prominence given to the matter is fully justified, assuming the facts are as repre- sented,and that the anticipations of those concerned are realised .The agent of this mechanical revolution is a new invention in connection with railway haulage. It appears that a Leeds engineer has brought out a novel valve gear which may be fitted on a locomotive at small cost, with the result that the haulage power is greatly augmented, and the coal consumption, if not actually reduced, is not in- increased. The invention is b-iing put to the test on the Great Northern Hailwa3, and the result is awaited with the keenest interest. If the experi-
merit made should prove satiifactory it may be

safely assumed that the principle will be adopted wherever steam traction is employed. For al- though the effect may not be to directly reduce the consumption of fuel on any particular engine, it follows that if it increases the haulage power of a locomotive, fewer engines will be in requisition on railway lines, and thus an immense saving of fuel will be made in the long run. The matter may be considered as of especial importance at a time when people are being told that the coal resources of the country are within measurable distance of being exhausted.

The new --- vaccination Bill has been rejected in considerable majority. the House of Lords by a feeling which at the present moment This measure VeDB practically an echo of the strong prevails throughout the country in favour of vac- cination. For, brave as anti-vaccinators appear to Rbe when they imagine there is nothin to fear, an epidemic has the effect of sending them to the vaccination stations in shoals. The Bill, if Passed, would simply have resulted in suppressing the so- called "conscientious objector " a year or so earlier than will be the case when the present tentative enactment expires next,year. The Clause was only intended as an experiment, running for five years from 1898, and is generally recognised as having failed. The fact that the Act would soon expire evidently weighed with the peers, who were per- haps well advised ta let the matter alone, it will suffice with many persons to know,on the authority of the President of the Local Government Board, as set forth in the House of Commons on Tuesday,that vaccinations which numbered 500,314 in 1898, in- creased to 669,349 in 1899, and to 677,655 in 1000; while the exemptions granted in 1808, numbering 203,341, were reduced in 1900 to 39,539, and in 1901 to 19,252. Under these circumstances, the Govern- ment may afford for the present to let well alone.

A WIDNES MAN KILLED IN TILE _ WEST FLOAT

On Monday, Thomas Dutton, aged nineteen, of James-street, Widnes, second mate on the steamer Sarah Brough, met with a fatal accident at the West Float, Birkenhead. qe was engaged working a winch, discharging gravel, when a pin broke, and the derrick fell upm his head. He was taken to the Seacombe Hospital, where life was pronounced extinct.

div.head: SALVATION ARMY, RUNCORN.
div.p: SALVATION ARMY, RUNCORN.

The self denial week in aid of the many worthy objects which are promoted by the Salvation Army will commence on March Ist. Donations will be received by any member of the corps. A juniors demonstration will also be held on Wednesday, to which we direct our readers special attention. For further particulars sae advt.

div.head: SEASONABLE GENEROSITY AT RUNCORN.
div.p: SEASONABLE GENEROSITY AT RUNCORN.

Mr W Scum, seamen's missionary, Runcorn, has, during the past few days,opsnen a soup kitchen at the Seamen's Institute, Station-road, for the benefit of the children of boarpeople, those whose parents have been thriwn out of work ill consegue see of the prevailing spell of hard weather, and also chil- dren who are iu indigent circumstances through the loss of the breadwinner On Monday nearly one hundred juveniles were entertained, besides a number of atults. Mn. JONES' MISSION.

In connec'ion with the above mission the first anniversary was held on Sunday, when Mr Millar, of Widnes, preached eloquent sermons in the after- noon and evening. On Monday the first annual tea was held. A goo I programme was afterwards pro- vided under the preiidency of Mrs Harrison. The following persons took part in the entertainment: —M Bennett, A Gatley,E Shone,C Jones,L Smith.G Hallwood, EHill and. others. A vote of thanks was afterwards given to Mesdames Harrison, Jones, Strange, Galley, Pindlow, Brown, Smith, Nfiss Haynes, and Messrs Brown and Bennett for their services. Mr Jones, the missiener, was responsible for the carrying out of the arrangements.

div.head: RUNCORN oYCLE CLUB,-A.NNUAL MRETING.
div.p: RUNCORN oYCLE CLUB,-A.NNUAL MRETING.

The annual meeting of the above club was held at Wilson's Hotel on Monday evening. Mr Criug- hall presided over a very good attendance, about 40 being present.—The financial report, preserved by the treasurer, Mr G Whinyates. showed a balance on the right side, after the year's working, of £3 Os 6d: This was considered extremely satisfactory. It was Stated that the past year had been a success- ful one, the membership having increased by 20— from 64 to 84.. It was rasolved to appeal for a stronger representation of the club on the Pro- visional Committee who have charge of the Cottage Hospital scheme. The following officers were elected for the ensuing year :—President, Mr S Taylor ; hon secretary. Mr W Booth ; hon treasurer, Mr George Whinyates ; captain of the Wednesday section, Mr George Whinyates; sub-captain. Mr W Lea; captain of the Saturday section,Mr C Glover; sub-captain, lr W Lea; captain of the Saturday section, Mr C Glover; sub-captain, Mr W Cooper. Last year's delegates for the N.C.U.. viz., Messrs W Booth and W Bankeq, were re-appointed. Hearty votes of thanks were accorded to the secretary and treasurer for their services during the past year. The chairman was also thanked for presiding.

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES. ----- [BY A CORRESPONDENT.]
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES. ----- [BY A CORRESPONDENT.]

The major portion of this week has been under the reign of the victorious King Frost. In Runcorn the cold has been more intense than has been ex- perienced for 'many years. The canal has bega blocked up for the first time this winter and traffic between Runcorn, the potteries, and the out- lying districts connected by water with Runcsrn has been for the time being abso- lutely impossible. Naturally this has occasioned great distress among that portion of the inhabitants who live in a perpetual state of hand to mouth existence, Mr Shaw, however, has come to the rescue of that portion who " go down to the sea in ships." :5 During the last few days the Mersey Mis- sion has been thrown open and over one hundred men, women and children have been fed with soup. Fortunately, the thaw has set in, which should bring in its wake increased necessity for labour, and this should obviate further steps ofor relief measures.

Runcornians generally and the police in particu- lar will be pleased to learn that on Wednesday there was a revival of what used to be an annual custom. At one period of local history the police social was regarded as an indispensable function but alas ! like Milton, in his time-honoured age, it has fallen on evil time. Nine years ago it fell into disuse through the supineness of a few indivi- duals which Seems to indicate so Mr Norman would argue that Runcorn has not beenlfor a period the " Merrie Runcorn" that it was in more respects than one. Those who note the alms of the times must confess that the canker of selfishness has certainly entered into our midst though whether this be in common with the majority of towns where competition holds all powerful sway, or whether Runcorn itself contains the seed of rottenness is a point open to discussion. At all events Messrs Cooke, Coventry and Wood have made a bold bid to resuscitate an annual so,:ial which should do much to cultivate that kind- liness of feeling between police and public which is essential to our welfare as a community. The gathering was so complete a success as to outshine any of its predecessors.

For the first time for at least nine years, the police of Runcorn were entertained on Wednesday evening at the Bethesda Lecture Hall. Up to a few years ago the annual police social was held with clock-work reeu- larity, bat, unfortunately, through some cause or other, the meeting was allowed to lapse, and it is only this year that a serious effort has been made to rejavenate an annual event which, at that time was second to none. The prime mover in again bringing t the fore this very necessary and enjoyabl 3 gathering may be said to be Mr F J Norman, J.P., whose interest in the welfare of the Police force and kindred organiza- tions is well-known. A strong committee consisting of Mes;r3 S Coventry, T Wood and T Cooke, gentlemen it may be added, who have previously had experience in this line were appointed to make the necessary arrangements for the re-establishment of the social and these gentlemen carried out their work with a thorough- ness which left nothing to be desired, the culmination of their efforts being seen on Wednesday evening. The room, it must be stated, had been very prettily decrr- ated with a motley collection of flags and streamers. The back of tbe platform, too, had been suitably draped while fronting the entrance to the hall was a large decorated emblem bearing the words " Welcome." Promptly at six o'clock a splendid knife and fork tea was served under the superintendence of Mesdames 9 Coventry, T Wood and T Cooke. At least fifty stalwart " gentlemen of the cloth" with their wives and ea eel- hearts, set down to pass an opinion on the good things under which the three large tables literally groaned and which had been set out with a delicacy of taste which left nothing to be desired. As soon as the inner man had been well fortified the room was speedily cleared of encumbrances by a number of willing workers and the deligh:ed constables sat down to a programme of the most varied and enter- taining description. Mr F J Norman presided and before the entertainment commenced, Mr Cooke announced that ho had several letters to read re the social. He wished, first of all, on behalf of the committee, to give them all a hearty welcome. He had received a letter from Superintendent Leah, deputy chief constable of Cheshire, who had been invited to attend and report to the chief constable. His reply was ,to the effect that as he had another appointment that ' evening he would ask to be excused. Be hoped,however, they would speed a mot enjoys hie evening. Before taking up this social they had had to communicate with Colonel Hammersley, who in reply approved of the plan and expressed his pleasure that the donors appreciated the work of the police so much as to provide them with a social. Sir Richard Broeke, J.P., had forwarded £2 towarde the expenses ; Mr S Taylor, J.P., £2 2s ; with the expression that the. social must never be allowed to lapse again ; Mr F J Norman, J.P.. £1 is;Mr A R Norman, J.P., £1 Is ; Mr Walter Timmins. J.P., 103 ; Mr H Reynolds, J.P., Helsby, £1 ; Mr John Ocllleston, J.P.,10 ;Mr E Imison J.P. 10; ; Mr R H Posnett, J.P.. 103 6cl ;Mr F A Frost. J.P., Grappenbil, £1 is. Mr A Thomas J. P. 104 61 :—The magistrates of Runcorn Petty Sessional Division had given the'..r hearty support to the entertainment, and it was the general •wish that the entertainments should be held 'in the future. lie was very proud to see Mr Norman oc3upping the chair that evenitar. He did not know of any magi.- trate who took a keener int'regt in the welfare of the pelice. (Applause.) Mr Norman had for some time been urging him to get up the social again and the fact that they were there that night was really 'due to Mr Norman. In view of this though Mr Norman was not the oldest magistrate on the Bench, they thought it only fair that he should be chairman. (Applause,) Superintendent Ennion said with the sanction of the Chief Constable it was with the greatest pleasure that he was with them. Ile thanked on behalf of the police ; all who had taken part in getting up the entertamme at for their kindness. While he had been ia Runcorn he lid always had the help of the magistrates and the public generally that he had never had in any other town. Go had pleasure in proposing a hearty vote of thanks to all who had taken part in inauguratiag, the social. Sergeant Gill seconded. Mr Coventry put the resolution te the meeting, which was carried unanimously._

Mr Norman, in responding on behalf of the donors said he was delighted to see S3rgeant Gill back a t his duties once more. He had bad a severe time of it dur- ing the past twelve months, but he hoped his strength and health would now continue favourable. He (the speaker) stood before them not only as a donor but, in la sense, as a natriarch. He did not recognise many old Runcornians there and he thought he could claim to be , the oldest Runcornian amongst them. Whether thor3 was a glamour cast over the past as he looked back upon it it was not for him to say but Runcorn did not seem to be the good, old, happy generous town of a few years ago. Everybody seemed to be ia the old days intent on making everybody Elie happy. He did not want for one moment to depreciate the old persons treat, inausursted many years ago, when poverty was not the qualification, but when it was rather regarded as a happy institution for bringing together all the old people for social entertainment and intercourse. The scavengers of the town were invited and the highest and the lowest met for once in happy union, and the sooner they got back to the o'd lines the better it would be. One of the best of these social gatherings was the one similar to that which they wire having that evening There were very few places inside or outside of the diviqien that`, had such a right royal time of it. Once at thi:Qiiarter Se,sioos Hammersley purposely went out of his way to soy hew gratified be was to think l bat the police force in the Runcorn Petty Sessional Divi lion were held in such high repute. This, Mr Norman continued indicated two things—ht the police did their duty and did 'le it well and that they did net exceed their duty. It was for this happy state of affairs that they, as law abiding citizens, were doing honour to the police. It was not the superintendent and the men in blue but the moral force of the people standing at their backs which kept law and order and they could net be too careful to maintain their high reputation. As custodians of the public weal they should cultivate and maintain that good feeling so n'eceesary bet aeon law-abiding citizens and the police force. When promo- tion Came to Superintendent Ennion he hoped he would regard Runcorn as one of the happiest places he had I ever visit.d. He hoped that the superintendent would spend a happy evening worthy of Runcorn an' its tradesmen. foe programme wail then opened by that charming song entitled " Mona " which was rendered with eklll and exprevion by Mr W Shaw. The same artiste also delighted the audience by a splendid rendering of "The flight of agee." On both occasions he was recalled. In conjunction with Miss Slinkin, who, was in Excellent voice, Mr Shaw was also heard to advantage in " Life's dream is o'er ! Farewell " for which they were recalled Miss Simkin further enhanced her reputation with her interpretation of " Angus McDonala " obliging the audience with the" O'd Umbrellalas an encore.%) The celebrated local humorist Mr W Jones was in evidence the whole of the evening with his quaint original sketches. His" Going to the Pintomime "was no hit of the evening and he was repeatedly recalled. Mr S Eanion's songs ware brimful of humour "It did go ' being exceptionally well rendered. The artiste was repeatedly recalled. " The gipsy's warning" was very prettily sung by Mrs Ennio!' who proved to be the possessor of a sweet soprano voice. The instru- mental selections by Miss Temperley, who plays the mandoline in a very skilful manner, produced quite an ovation tor the artinto, which was thoroughly deserved. A local elocutionist in the person of Mr T Inman who is somewhat new to Runcorn audiences made quite a reputation for himself by his meritorious treatment of the sketch entitled " The Bashful man." On several occasions he was recalled and kept the audience in a continuous state of merrimont Mr W Cooke A.R.C,O. accompanied and to his accomplished touch may be added much of the succsss of the averring.

At the close of the social Inspector Ezerton proposed a vote of thanks to ail %visa had helped and participated in the concert. He had never bean treated better than at Runcora In any part of the county and he per- sonally thanked all concerned. Sergeant Brewster, seconded and remarked, in Alm course of a somewhat witty speech, that he had neve enjoyed himself at an entertainment so much before The resolution being carried, Mr Wood responded. "Supper was at terwards served, progressive games etc, following, which concluded as pleasant a social as has been held in Runcorn for some time. The proceed- ings from first to last were a proneunced success and the Wghest eulogium would scarcely be sufficient to express the credit which devolves OR the committee for the manner in which they perfected the arrangements.
ALARMING FIRE AT NEWTON.

On Saturday evening a fire broke out in the Con- gregational Church, Newton, which but for the early discovery and prompt action taken to deal with it would have had the most disastrous conse- quences, in fact it is not too much to say that had the fire not been noticed when it was nothing could have saved the whole building. In consequence of the frost, and extreme cold weather, the chapel- keeper was instructed to keep a good fire in the heating apparatus in order to make the chapel com- fortable for Sunday. He carried out these instruc- tions, with the result that the hot air pipes became too hot, and a gas pipe in the organ loft, running very close to the heating pipes, was melted, and the gas escaping it became ignited, with the result that the woodwork was set on fire. The brother- in-law of the caretaker noticing an unusual light in chapel drew the attention of his relative to it. The caretaker at once rushed out, and on getting into the chapel found the organ loft in flames. He raised an alarm, and a number of men at once gave willing assistance, buckets of water being poured on the flames. The hose belonging to the District Council was brought into use, but when it was fastened on to the hydrant, the water spurted out all over it, and was of no earthly use. A policeman was despatched to McCorquodale's works for a reel, but before be returned the fire had been extin- guished. The organ casing was damaged, and it is expected the interior has suffered from the water. Service was held in the schoolroom on Sunday. ¶1 he damage is estimated at about £6O, but it is Covered by insurance.
VOLUNTEER BILL AT NEWTON-LE-WILLOWS.

King's Liverpool Regiment took place at the Town Hall last Friday eveninw, and proved to be one of the most successful ever held. As usual the decorations were of an especi- ally attractive character, the embellishment of the platform being quite a work of art.- Flags and bunting were lavishly used, and many striking and original effects were produced. Stars of bayonets and other military devices, adorned the walls. This work was entrusted to Mr Davenport, whose admirable execution of it gave entire satisfaction. The proceedings opened at nine o'clock some 40 couples having then assembled, and the music which was new and pretty, was supplied by Mr Pearson's band. The duties of M.C.'s were credit- ably performed by Lance-Sergeant Pullen and Cor- poral Anderson. A programme of 24 dances was gone through. The proceedings broke up about half-past five o'clock. EXAMINERFIIE FRI A 1 FEBRUARY 21 1909 ••••1 - RUNCORN CONSTABLES' ANNUAL EARLESTOWN & NEV TON. I NOTES BY THE WAY AT SOCIAL EVENING. EARLESTOWN. P.S.A. The weekly meeting of the Earlestown ani.Dis- trict P.S.A. Society was held in the Co-operative Hall, Earlestown on Sunday afternoon. Mr Ellis presided, and an addresi was given by Mr E J George. Vocal items ware given by Miss M Part- ington and recitations by Miss M Watkins. Miss Williamson presided at the piano. EARLESTOWN WESLEYAN CYCLING CLUB. A social re-union in connection with this dab Cook place on Wednesday evening in the Wesleyan Lecture Hall. There was not a large attendance, but an enjoyable evening was spent, A lantern en- tertainment was given, and a number of photo- graphic elides were shown, descriptive of the places visited by the club in its runs. Songs were given and a number of games were heartily raken part in. VIADUCT WORKS CASUALTIES Oa Thursday, at the Viaduct Works, Earlestown, belonging to the London and North-Western Rail- way Company, whilst a waggon was being lifted in the waggon seop, she jack supped out of its place, and the waggon fell on a man named Geerge Parker, whilst the jack struck another man named David Pnillips on the right foot, and seriously injured it. ! Parker had his right leg broken and slight injuries to the head. Both men were taken home. NEWTON IN-MAKERFIELD VICTORIA MEMORIAL COTTAGE HOSPITAL. At a meeting of the committee in connection with 1 the above held on Wednesday, February 19th, (Mr T Ormand in the chair), Mr s Driag, joint hon sec- retary, tendered his resignation, owing to pressure of business.—A resolution was pissed by the com- mittee accepting with regret Mr Dring's resignation, also expressing their high appreciation of the ser- vices he had rendered toward e the movement.— Mr Dring, briefly responded, thanking the committee for kind words expressed. AN EX-EARLESTOWN FOOTBALLER WRESTLES FOR THE INTER,NATIONAL CHAMPIONSHIP. 1 At Buffalo, on Friday, a wrestling match for the international Championship, which carridd with it a prize of several thousand dollars, took place between Tom Jenkins, of Cleveland, and Jim Parr, who was billed as the English Champion. The former succeeded in throwing Parr twice' and was proclaimed winner. " Chutty " Parr is well-known in Earlestown, where he played in the local foot- hill team for several years. SEQUEL TO A FIGHT AT EARLESTOWN.—SERIOUS CHARGE. At the Warrington Occasional Court on Tuesday, before Ms A Frost, Peter Williamson, an iron- worker of the Vulcan, Earlestown, was charged with inflicting grievous bodily harm upon James Winward, ironworker, also of the Vulcan, at Newton, on the 16th inst.—Winward, was unable to appear, being detained in the Warrington In- firmary. Evidence was given t o the effect that the injured man and another man were fighting, and while they were on the floor Williamson kicked Winward, fracturing three or four of his r,bs.— Prisoner was remanded to the Newton Petty Sessions to be held on the 27th. DEATH OF An OLD NEWTONIAN. Many friends and acquaintances of Mr W Berry of Wigan-road, Ashton and late of Newton-le- Willows will regret to hear of his death at the age of 68 years, which took place on Saturday last. He had been indisposed for some time and a frequent visitor at his bethide was the Rev time, Allatc. Mr Berry:was exceptionally well known in Newton,and he had earned the respect and esteem eta numer- ous circle of friends. Toe funeral took place on Tuesday, the body being interred at the Newton Cemetery, amid manifestations of sympathy, Wreaths were sent by Mr and Mr C II Berry, Mr and Mrs W 11 Berry, Mt and Mrs A E Berry, Mr and Mrs Ii Berry, Mrs B )artim in, kit' an 1 Mrs Alderson, Mr and Mrs Foulds, Mr and Mrs Ash, Mr and Mrs Hibbert, Mr and Mrs C Owen, and Mr Swift (lawyer) Liverpool, all of whom were present at the funeral. Tee service was performed by the Rev James Allatt. THE FROST. The keen weather has been much enjoyed in Earlestown and Newton, and skating has been freely indulged in. Happily, however,lthere have not been any accidents. Newton Lake has been quite safe, but the ice was decidedly rough, and considerably marred the pleasure. The surface was crowded with people from the surrounding districts on Saturday afternoon, and on Sunday there were some hundreds of people on the ice, although the numbers of those skating were not nearly so large as on the previous day. A sketiag match on Sun- day afternoon was something of a fiasco but it was only taken part in by the rougeer element. A thaw set in on Tuesday night, and the safest thing to do will be to refrain trom venturing on the ice at Newton. Accompanying the thaw have been plenty of burst pipes in private house, mostly in connection with the bath arrangements, and plumbers have been kept exceptionally busy. A MAN'S LEG AND FOOT CUT OFF AT EARLESTOWN. Oa Saturday afternoon a bottle packer named William Jackson, in the employ of Messrs C B F Borron and Co.. Newton, met with a very serious accident as the result of which he has lost a good portion of one leg, and the foot of another. He was going tewards his home in Athol-street, after finish- ing work, and as a near cut, walked along Messrs. Evans and Co.'s privat3 line, running behind Crow- lane. It was very foggy at the time, and it is sup- posed he fell over the rails just as one of Messrs Evans and Co.'s engines was propelling some waggons along the line. Unfortunately he did not fall clear of the railseland Vie wheels of some of the waggons passed over both his legs. Dr Latham was sent for and did what he could under the cir- cumstances, and ordered the man's removal to Hay- dock Cottage Hospital. He was put into an empty waggon and immediately conveyed to the hospital Jackson is a married man, with a family of 7 hildren, and he is progressing as well as can be , xpected. EARLESTOWN CO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY. The 165th quarterly meeting lef the members of this society was held in !the Co-operative Hall on Monday evening. Mre'D Forrester presided,but there was only a meagre attendance of members. The ' report of the committee showed that there had been a further substantial increase in business. The cash receipts were £12,101 14s, being an increase over last quarter of £1,190 Hs 9id and compared with the corresponding period last year showed an increase of .£1.574 Os 61. The net profits realised were £1,822 Ss 31, which it was proposed to dis- pose of by payiag a nividend of 3s in the .e to members, absorbing £1760 183 61, and the balance of £6l 9s 9d to be divided as follows :—£lo to Workmen's Compensation Fund ; .£lO to dividend reserve fund and the balance £4l 93 93 to contingent fund. During the quarter 60 new mem- bers had been admitted, 27 had withdrawn, leaving ' 1761 on the register, 1312 of whom had brought in checks. After discussions on various items of ex- penditure, the balance sheet was adopted. Mr D Forrester was re-elected president, and Mr T Hegel- den was re-elected auditor. Messrs E Jones and T Cave were nominated for re-election to the corn- ' =Wee The report of Mr Judson, delegate to the wholesale society's quarterly meeting was sub- mitted and adopted, and the committee's recom- mendations as to delegates' expenses were agreed It.. The question of holding a field day in the summer for the children of members was intro- duced and discussed, power being ultimately given the committee to make needful arrangements. A grant of .£5 to the Newton-in-Makertield Lecture Committee was agreed to. This was all the busi- ness.
[BY A CORRESPONDENT]

We have had quite enough frost and snow in this district to last for some considerable time to come. Its severity can be gauged by the fact that Newton Lake has been frozen suficiently to admit of thousands of people skating on its surface It is several years since the whole of the lake was frozen over and consequently the enjoyment was entered into with greater zest. People flocked to Newton from all round the dis- trict,a good number coming:even from Warrington Die ice,however, was very rough,an I it would have compensated the skaters if they had got a few out• of-work men with brooms, to sweep it, and after- wards passed round the hat. Now all is over, and the thaw has quickly transformed the lake into a sheet of water again.

The coming of the frost has not been unattended with accidents. An oldlady 85 years of age slipped and fell on the frozen road, breaking one ot her legs in three places. In her case the accident may have a fatal termination. On Saturday a man slipped and fell on Hay(lock Colliery line, and unfortunately for him one of the Colliery engines just at that time was taking a number of wagons to the depot, and before the man could get out of the way the train was on him, the result being that he has lost a goodly portion of both his legs. A middle-aged lady slipped on the frozen snow in Crow-lane and broks her leg, and another woman fell in the Sack-yard of her house, and in saving , herself, broke one of her wrists. In other ways the frost has caused annoyance and inconvenience chiefly to householders woo are blessed with baths. Many have had their pipes frozen up since .the advent of the frost, and when the thaw set in the burets were numerous, and the result has been , flooded dwellings and more work than the plumbers could very well get through. Fortunately however, there has been no such thing as bursting boilers.

The necessity for a properly equipped fire brigade in cannection with the town was never more exemplified than on Saturday night when the Congregational Church at Newton had a narrow escape of being destroyed by fire. The organ loft, where the fire originated is of pitch pine, as also is the casing of the organ, and the chapel roof. Had the discovery been delayed another five minutes the fire would have got such a hold of the timber, that nothing whatever coud have saved the build- ing. A reel belonging to the District Council was obtained, but when it was attached to the hydrant the water, instead of coming through the nozzle, spurted out all over the pipe, and it was of no earthly use, except to drench anyone who stood near. The men, however, who gave their aid' worked like Trojans, and with a copious bucket service, were able to master the flames, and eventu- ally extinguish them. The C4uncil have had the question of establishing a town's fire brigade under cansideration,but it does not seam to advance much further than the considering stage, and one of these days some important building will become a prey to the flames because of the sence of proper appliances. ab

div.head: SHOCKING BURNING FATALITY AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: SHOCKING BURNING FATALITY AT EARLESTOWN.

01 Monday adternom a burning fatality of a p,culiariy shocking character took place at Farlesto Mary Rowley, five years of age, daughter of Wiliam Rowley, a carpenter employed at the London and North Western Company's Waggon Works, and residing in Crow-lane West,Earlcstown, was left in a bedroom wita other children in which there WIS a fire burning. For s rme time they played about without mishap, but the mother, having to leave the house to sperk to a person in the roadway, heard screams, and immediately returning to toe hous3 found the child Mary in flames. Sae succeeded in extinguishing the fire with blankets, but the poor girl was horribly burnt. Dr Mouncey was sent for, but seeing the charred condition of the child's body, he held out no hope whatever of recovery, and 1 the girl died in great agony shortly before midnight. THE INCHTE3I'. STRONG REMARKS I.IT THE CORONER. The inciu(st was held on Tuesday afternoon at the Town Hail, EtiLstown, by Mr S Brighouse, coroner. Jeannette Howley, the mother of the deceased said she was the wife of William Rowley, who was employed as a wagon maker at the Viaduct Works and resided at 105, Crow—lane, West, E trlestown. The children were away from school o a Monday afternoon, having been granted a holiday. She put the four children in one of the bedrooms to play, and made a fire in the room. She did this in order Co keep them from going on the ice. From one of the windows she saw a woman named Carlin coming along the roadway, and she left the house for a few minutes to ask Mrs Carlin if she could spare her a bit of parsley. She was talking to her for a few minutes, and on her son William running out and tell- ing her Mary was on fire, she rushed into the house, and into the bedroom and found.deceafe 1 in flames. She immediately obtained some blankets from a bed and.vvrapped them round the child and then seat for the doctor. In answer to the Coroner, witness said there were four children in the bedroom, viz : William aged 8, Lillie May aged 7, Phyl is aga d 4 and deceased. Ten minutes before the accident occurred sbe was in the bedroom and the children were alright then. There was no fire guard, neither was taere a fender on the hearth. To grate was a very small one. The Coroner asked the witness if she had heard the rumours that were circulating round the town, and on c3iving a reply in the negative, he informed her that people were saying she,waa drunk at the time of the accident.

Witness strongly denied tais and said she ha I not seen a drop of drink all that day. The Coroner said it was further rumoured that she had no dinner ready for her husband "Mel he came home at one o'clock, and that as a coniequence they had quarrelled. Witness denied this and sail that her hugbtod simply blamed her for keeping the children at home, but that he did not say anything further when he knew they had a holiday. The Coroner said she must admit that it was a very dangerous thing to leave four children in a room in the way she did. Witness i id she had only left them for ten minutes. _

The Coroner said one minute was quite enough for an accident to happen. Eta could only say that te sooner the legislature stepped in with an Act for making fire guards compulsory, the better it WAIld be for every- body. In answer to the foreman, witness said deceased's outer garments were made of fiaonslette. William Rowley, aged 8, brother of deceased said his sister was stood near the fire twisting her pinafore and although ho told her not to play with the fire, she got to near and her clothas became ignited. He then ran out for his mother.

PC Clarke said there bad been a lct of talk amongst the neighbours about Mrs Rowley being drunk at the time of the accident, but Ile saw no signs of drink when he went to tho house about 2.45, During con- versation with her husband he learned that Mrs Rowley wag drunk when he came home to dinner at one o'clock and they had differences. She struck him and he struck her back, and she then threw a kettle at him, but no injury Wa3 inflicted, Some time ago an inspector to the N.S.P.C.C. visited the home and warned the women as to her drunken habits.

_ In reply to the Coroner witness said that Mrs Rowley's tile about going to see Mrs Carlin was plausible onoogh He did not think she was going for drink. In summing up the Coroner referred to the conduct of Mrs Rowley in leaving four children in a room oy themselves with a fire in the room and no fender nor guard near it, There was no doubt that at 1 o'clock she was drunk and be thought that she was in some measure to blame fo: the accident.

The jury were left to consider their verdict which they eventually brought in as " Accidental Deach and asked the Coroner to !severely censure thewoman." Mrs Rowley was again brought into the room and again addressing her the Coroner said that it was very little use his speaking to such women as bet. She ought to b 3 thoroughly ashamed of herself to allow four chil- dren to be in a room like that unattended. He thought that she ought to save a bit of money from the drink and buy a fire guard with it. Her husband was getting £2 51 per week and this was plenty to allow of fire guards being purchased, In concluding the Coroner asked her how she would like to be burned like her child and dismissed her by saying " Go sway you cruel woman."

div.head: NOTES ON UAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON UAMES AND ATHLETICS.
RUGBY FOOTBALL.
By `i Ovalist."

Notwithstanding the vigorous nature of the weather, Warrington managed to get one of their League fix- tures played off last Saturday, when they met the wooden-spoonists of the League at Brighouse. The Rangers' ground had been protected by a covering of hops, but it was still hard, and scarcely suitable for the keen game which was played. Rather than have any postponement however the teams decided to play, and Warrington, at any rate will probably not be sorry seeing that they got a welcome two points out of the match.

It is rather a curious circumstance that Warrington should win without Isherwood and Fish, while Lanca- shire lost with their assistance. Both results were a bit surprising, and the last one very much so. War. rington, of course, ought to win at Brighouse, but with such ,:rood men as Burgess, Isherwood, Fish and Board- man absent, their chances were somewhat discounted. The rest the team has had,however,has done them good, and they had far the best of a hard g,ame.The points in Warrington's favour would have been considerably more if the substitutes had only taken some of the easy chances of scoring which were offered them. Once Swift got over the 'line with an apparently fair try which was disallowed, and eventually Hallam won the match with a penalty kick, which sent the ball over the bar. It is rare iiideed that Warrington have such a stroke of luck, and the two points gained on Saturday compensate somewhat for those 'lost at Swinton in a similar way.

For a great pari; of the time Warrington had only 14 men, Duckworth retiring early with a damaged leg. Edmonds worked hard behind the pack and gave a very good account of himself. In fact his display all through was highly satisfactory. Later on the home team also lost a half-back, Armitage having to leave the field with an injured —reported broken—s oulder. Being once more on a numerically level footing War- rington played up well and for the rest of the time Brighouse were kept hard on the defensive.

Hallam and Dickenson also played an excellent game, and there were indications that bath are coming back into their best form. Warrington may finish up with a decent position in the League, for the team is likely to be a formidable one when it is at full strength.

The county match at Hull was a great disappoint- ment to Lancashire people, who never expected that the Yorkshire forwards would so turn the tables tha t the Palatine team would be beaten fore and aft as they undoubtedly were. It was Lancashire's off-day, for in addition to missing the services of Valentine and Hogg most of the other backs played far below form, and the honours of the day really fell to Isherwood and Fish, wholwere always smart and reliable. The Yorkshire men made no secret of their plan of campaign,and they carried it out. The forwards completely smashed up the Lancashire combination after the first quarter of an hour, and Own the home backs got going to a lively tune. Tom Davies's inclusion at centre strengthened the weakest place and the ex•Oldhamite gave a masterly display. He and Watty Davies were in fine form, and the same can be said of the halves (Grace and Marsden) and Taylor, the full back. Yorkshire won easily and won well, and Lancashire will have to sing small for a bit.

Cheshire are now the county champions, owing to the fact that they beat Yorkshire and Cumberland and drew with Lancashire. The Runcorn-Stockport com- bination have played with splendid determination all through, and the men fully deserve the honour and gold medals which have been won as a result of the county tournament for 1901-2. They have something to thank Yorkshire for all the same. The odds would have been on Lancashire had the two teams met again .

Warrington have supplied three backs to the County team this season, Isherwood, Fish and Dickenson all having represented the County Palatine in one or other of the matches, while Hallam and Boardmanhave been on the reserve. lam glad that Isherwood, in parti- cular has at last had a chance, and all the critics speak well of him. Fish, by the ws.y,has played in all county matches this season.

Saturday also saw the downfall of Halifax, who were handsomely beaten at home by Hunslet. How erratic some of these Yorkshire teams are! Batley came south and gave Oldham a terrible fright, the " rough-yeds " only drawing level in the last five minutes.

The Warrington crowd will be glad to hear that Allen is well again. having quite recovered from the injuries he had sustained internally. He expresses himself St again and has been chosen to partner Edmonds against Widnes to-clay.

To-day's match is one in the South-West Lancashire League, Widnes being Warrington's opponents. At present these two clubs have the best chance of obtain- ing the honours in this competition and if Warrington only avenge the defeat sustained at Widnes they will have an excellent prospect for the South-West Lanca- shire Championship. Nobody in Warrington doubts that they will defeat the leaders of the Lancashire Senior ...,ompetition at Wilderspool even though the latter won in the first engagement. That game was a most miserable one, played on a shockingly wet day, and with Warrington handicapped by the absence of the pick of the team. Yet Widnes only won somewhat luckily by two goals to a try, and I fully expect War- rington to rub in that reverse without any compunction to-day.

The chosen team is as follows : Hallam, full back; Fish, Isherwood, Dickenson, and Harris, threequarters ; Edmonds and Allen, half backs; Boardman, Morrison, Edmondson, Fell, Taylor, Swift, Ashton, and Jolley, forwards. One change is to be noticed from last week's selection, Allen coming in vice Duckworth, injured. I am glad to see Allen back again. Though not a brilliant half he is always a hard worker and abso- lutely reliable. lie should form a very effective worker of the scrimmage for Edmonds, who is expected to make openings and, 1 understand, can do so.
Fish was injured sligh' ly in the county match, a rough tackle damaging his arm, but he is expected to be fit for today's long looked for tussle.

div.head: LOCAL TEA MEETINGS
div.p: LOCAL TEA MEETINGS
St. JOHN'S PRE3BYIERIAN CEIIIRCH.

St. John'a schoolroom was gaily decorated with flags and bunting on Thursday ever:ling when the annual con- gregational tea meeting and entertainment were held. A capital tea was provided and thoroughly enjoyed by atoat 159 members of the congregation and friends. the tables tieing nresided over by Mesdames Milne. Miller, Lockerbie,Kirkpatrick, Hawthorne. W S Neil, Walker, S McDowell and Ditchtleld and Miss Duncan, A large nimb,r of trays were received, the following sending over 53 :--Tne Diouty-Mayor (Alderman Roberts). Alderman Heaton. Mr A II Cro.fiald, Mr W Owen, Messrs Greened Whitler and Company. Messrs the Mersey White Lead Co , Dr Parker, Messrs F Sinirh, C Suolow, 9 Neil, J Neil, Milne, McDowell and McLartv Mrs McDowell and Miqs J Tinsley. After the tables had been cleared an entertainment was held. the Rev T H Scott of Manchester,presiding over the proceedings. The choir opened the concert with a part song " Killarney " which was creditably rendered. They gave two other part songs during the evening, the one " tilPrp my baby" being exeeptionallo well submitte 1. Rig gave two hUmormis recitations with great success, being enthusiastically recalled for his second effort. Mr M Owen, and Mr K,noon delighted the audience with sow's. gMr Arnott played several Scotch airs on the vi lin, being heartily reca!le.d. During an interval the R.v T H Scott gave a brief address on the progress ,f the church and ur..,el upon the members thellesdrability of relreaent d elected on the suatentation fund in connection with the Presbyterian churches. He pointed out that for a church to get on the'stubentation fund the synod desired that they Fhould send £BO per year towards the ministers stipend. When he, as a moderator of the Church, first saw their annual balance sheet some twelve months ago he noticed that after trit.efing elt ordinary expenditure, exclusivecf the ministers' stipend they had a working balance of £29 left. In order to make up the amount necessary to carry on the work of the-Criurch they had mad, a successful application for a grant to the Horne Mission Com- mittee. Looking at the next balance sheet he saw that after meeting all ordinary expenditaire, exclusive of the minister's stipend, they had a working balance left nf £7O a year: They wantel to increase that £7O to £BO by o.2toher and thereby get cri the sustect Oren fund. The speaker vvnt on to point out the.advantages arising out of the Suatentat'on Fund, awl in conclusion said ho hoped—nay, he believed that every member of that con- gregation would vie with each other in doing something to help on their Church. (Applause). Mr Barclay also snoke of the value of the Sustentation Fund. For every £3O sent to the fund they received £l5O, for every'pound over and above the £BO they re- ceived in return 30s. He suggested that the easiest way to raise the £l.O per year requisite for them to get on the fund would be to form a committee of two ladies and one gentleman tn gather in the subScrirti one to the fund by means of house to house visitation. each mere- b.er tr 4 agree to contribute some small sum—say one penny per week—in addition t) what they already coc- tribute& If that were done the result of the com- mittee's efferts would not only be the raising of money but it would tend to knit toe members no' r' strongly together in their work for the church. (Applause.)
The Northern Education League and the Warrington Si 1..

At the monthly meeting of the Executive Com- mittee of the Northern Education Lealzus. held at Leeds the provisions of the Warrington Elucation Bill were considered, and the opinion was express- ed that in spire of some good features in the measure, its promotion was likely to assist the Government in interfering with School Boards. It was reported that an important resolution of Education would be submitted at Bradford to the National Council of Evangelical Free Churches. Dr Aired also stated that a National Conference of the Free Churches would be subsequently sum- moned. The Chairman earnestly addressed the Committee on their duty of fighting every propo4al of the Government calculated to injure Education, weaken direct popular control, and endow sec- tarian dogmas az.d coercion out of taxes and. rates.

GROBS ILLTREATMENT OF A HORSE—. HoTHING BUT SKIN AND BONES" At the Warrington County Petty zessions, on Wednesday morning before Mr:CI- Comber and other magistrates,Wllliam Nicholson, 66 Lodge-lane Werpool, was charged with hew- ing ill-treated a horse by working it whilst in an unfit, state at Rixton on February sth ; and William Nelson, furniture remover land 3, Windsor-view Lodge-lane Liverpool, was charged with causing the some to be worked.— Nizbolson did not appear and a warrant was issued fr his arrest. Nelson pleas.! not guilty.— Mr Stee'. who prosecuted on behalf of the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, said Cid Ni2ho:son Was sent out on the 3rd inst with a two-horse van to take a load of furniture 'mom Liverpool to 7tlandyster. He was on his way back at hslf-past twelve on th • morning of the F.th inst. when ha was met by Po ice-constable Clarke satloned at. Caxton. who found one horse attached to the van. and ano'her lying on the rcadway groaning. On examining the latter horse it was found to be an aged bay gelding in an extremely poor condition, and Was nothing but skin and bones. It was quite exhausted, and unable to walk, and it took almost half an hour to get tt on its feet. Nicholson told the constable that he had had the horse behind the van and it had dropped in the roadway He did not know that the horse had droppai until the driver of the mail-cotch had told him that it was lying in the roadway. Nicholson said he did not want to work the animal and told his employe (Nelson) so, but his had either to take the horse oat or get "tbe sack" The constable advised him to take the horse to a neighbouring farm that of a Mr. -dater, and defendant ! said he would as soon as he could get the animal up I After great diffieulty that WAS accomolidied, and , tea animal was taken to Mr. olateea farm. It I staggered as it went. It was put into a stable and I immediately commenced eating sane straw which was lying about. It appeared not to have bad any mod for a consider- able time. Tho following morning, prior to a visit of In-pector Print, Mr Slater's sou took the horse out for a drink and it I fell down in the yard throu ea weakness. On the 7th February the Inspector visited Nelson at Liverpool, and he said that when the horselstarted on the journey it was in fair eondition It was, submitted Mr Steel, impossible for , the horse to get Into such a condition in four days The horse afterwards died, and on the 9th it was examined by Mr Dixon,veterinary surgeon, who said dealt) Was due to ex- haustion trona want at food, combined with overwork In his (Mr Dixon's) opinion it was a case of gross,wanton,cruelty.— Styli-lance bearing on/ this etatenent was given —Defendan, said that when the lnrse lent Live p it was in fair con- dition, and plenty of food WAS sent witn it. He contended that Nicholson Was to blame, —the Ch Orman Said the Bench did no; consider the case against Nelson an aggravated one. It seamed clear that he sent load with the horse, but at the same time it would have been better to have kept the animal at home. He would be fined 13s and costs.—An. advocate's fee was allowed.

There WaS a fairly large attendance of spectators at Brig- house to witness till return match between the Rangers and Warrington. The ground had been protected with hop . ,and there was also a slight covering of snow, but underneath the ground was very bard, and it was not at all suitable for a keenly contested game. Warrington were abort of Nish, Isberwcod and 13oardnaan, who had been called upon to go to Hull.

Swift started the game for Warrington by kicking uphill. to which Hoiroyd made a good return. and Brighouse pressed. Dickenson reit ved with a tlne rim, and even play ensued ai. the centre. Duckworth, me of the Warrington men, had to retire with a leg badly damaged. Up to half- time no points were registered by either side. •

The re-start vas made by Miller, and hope was strong among the local partisans that Brighouse would win. Loch- man dribbled finely, and pfactically saved Brighouse at a critics! moment. Baker, a few moments later, was instru- mental in preyeeting Hallam from haying a run in. The visitors played up strongly, and the attack on the Brighouse line was vigorous and well sustained Warrington had several narrow shaves of crossing the Brighouae line, and but for the final passes going wrong they must have scored. A little later Hallam scored a penalty goal, a feat which won the match for his side. Miller re started for Brighouse, and soon after A,rrnitage (Brighouse, retired with a broken shoulder. Warrington pressed In the final stages, and Brig- house were fortunate In preventing further scoring. Unveiling a Memorial Window at
Newton.

A special service was held at St Peter's Church, Newton-le-Willows, on Sunday afternoon, when the handsome stained g1a.,5 window placed in the west end of the church as a memorial to the late Rev Herbert Monk, M A, for 28 years vicar of the parish, was un- veiled by Dr J W Watkins, in the absence of the Rev Canon Peorhyn, who had previously Woo announced to perform the ceremony. There was a fairly largo congro- gation. The service opened with the anthem. " Send out thy light," and while the Te Daum was being sung, the Year, Dr Watkins, and the choir proceeded to tee west end where special d-dicatory prayers were said. ' Dr Watkins unveiled the window and expressing at the earns time the following w,srds To the glory of God, , Ira the name of the Holy frinity, and in the faith of Jesus Christ. and in the memory of Thy servant Her- bert, for 23 years vicar of this parish, this window is now unveiled." Pulling a cord, the canvas fell aside, and the magnifizent window was revealed to the con- gregation. Alter a sine interval the recessional hymn. —" 0 Light, whose beams illumine all," was sung. This was followed by the prayer for the Church Militant and the hymn " For all the saints who from their labours rest.'—The Vicar delivered a short address based on the text, " Their works do follow them." —A a:Ref.:non was afterwards taknn, and it re.alizad £25 s, which will be devoted to the Tower Fund.

Aural statistics show that the great majority of cases I of Deafness are the result of diseaas attacking the cavity of the middle ear. This cavity, which contains many of the structures essential to the eransmisaion of sound to tee brain, is 89 elleply seated within the bones of the skull that specialists wore for a long time unable to apply the treatment necessary to cure the middle ear disease, and thus restore hearing. Happily, this diffi- culty has been OVOiCOMS by the treatment devised by Dr Droaet, and the proof of this is to be f iund in the fact that tee Editor of the " Journal for the Deaf " is now publishing as a Supplement a moethly record of the cures accomplished by the Drouet Institute. St. Helens Cable Company and German Machinery. . .

On Saturday, in the Court of Appeal, consisting of the Master of the Rolls and Lord Justice Mathew, in the case of Weiss and Another v the St Helens Cable Company, Limited, the defendants appealed from an order of Mr Justice Jelf, in chambers, by which he varied an order as to the costs of the action made by the taxing master. It appeared that the plaintiffs,vvho carry on business in German v.brought an action to recover a sum of about £1,700, balance alleged to be due on a quantity of machinery sup- plied to the defendant. By way of defence the defendants sot up a counter-claim claiming damages for late delivery, and they further contended that there were serious defects in the machinery, for which they were entitled to some consideration The case came before the official referee at, Liver- pool, who gave judgment for the plaintiffs on the claim in full, and for the defendants on the counter- claim for £550, and directed that the plaintiffs should have the costs of the claim and the defend- ants the costs of the counterclaim. On the matter coming up for taxation, the taxing master divided the costs into two parts. The plaintiffs appealed to Mr J ustice Jelf, who held that the master was wrong in not allowing the plaintiffs the costs of their expert witnesses. Hence the present appeal. The appeal was dismissed with costs. Temporary Authority. At the Cunty Borozigh Polics Court on Monday Mr Edward Melia, of the firm of Daniel Melia and, Co., was granted temporary authority to sell spirits at the company's establishment in Horsemarket- street in lieu of the lace Mr John L Hall.

Wycliffe British Schools. The report on the past year's work at these schools has just been issued. The managers are pleased to state that the average attendance in the Upper Department increased by 28, being 428 for the Year, while in the Infants' Department there was a decrease of 4, or an average of 139. This fact, together with the knowledge that so far as the new year has gone the attendance is still lower does not emphasize the great need of 'additional infants' accommodation in this district for which so much agitation is taking place. The following extracts are taken from the annual report of His Majesty's Inspector, Mr E. L. Phelns— Mixed school " Discipline is well and quietly main- tained and the organization carefully attended to. The work is generally intelligent and reaches a highly creditable level of efficiency." Infants' school "The instruction in the Infants' school is carefully planned and given with fairly good effect."

Preparations for the May Day Procession. Preparations for the May Day PrOcession of Horses have already commenced. A preliminary meeting of the committee was held at the Lion Hotel on Monday afternoon, Sir Gilbert Greens,ll, Bart., presiding over a good attendance which in- cluded Alderman II Roberts, II essrs Munro, I Wynne Jones, Fulton Smith, Newton, Fletcher and G Venn (secretary).—lt was decided to hold the procession on Saturday. May 4th, the general opinion being that this day would be convenient for all concerned. A short diecussion took place as to the advisability of giving prizes or holding a dinner for the carters taking part in the procession—The Secretary said that no prizes were given last year as the procession took place about a week after the Erst meeting of the Committee. The Chairman expressed the opinion that the prizes should be given for the grooming of the horses and cleaning of the harness &c.—Alderman Roberts thought the question as to the extent of prize-giving would in- troduce an element of discord. Personally he would prefer to subscribe for a dinner to the carters —Ultimately it was decided that Messrs Pretty, Pierpoint, Newton, Isherwood and Venn should constitute a sub-committee to obtain information as to the rules appertaining in respect to the prize giving &c,. in connection with the London, Liverpool, and Manchester processions and report to the Committee—This was all the business.

A baker in the Avenue de Is Rapublique, Paris.whoso I preMisee have for a long time been infested with rats, borrowed a cat two days ago in the hope of getting rid 1 of the rats. At night the baker and his wife were awakened by a terrible din and the sound of falling glass, and going downstairs, they saw the cat leaping about the shop in a most extraordinary fashion. Thinking the animal was mad the proprietor called in the police, who shot it dead. A veterinary surgeon made a post mortem examination of the carcase, and it was discovered that the cat had not been mad, but only intoxicated, having eaten half-a-dozm sponge cakes soaked in rum which She had found on the counter.
