div.p: WARRINGTON CYCLING CLUB.

A Successful Season Reviewed. Parade Suggested for This Year. A very satisfactory state of affairs was reported to the members of the Warringten Cycling Club at their annual meeting which was held at the Patten Arms Hotel on Thursday last week. Judging by the aft Affi- ance on such a bitterly cold night, the interest taken by the members in the doings of the club, sheava no signs of waning and, under the presidency of Mr J Critchleyethe proceedings passed off most harmoniously. A SUCCESSFUL SEASON—IN VERESTING REPORT BY SHE SECRETARY. The SECRETARY (Mr E. Pickavance, jun.), presented the sixteenth annual report and at tile outset said it gave him groat pleasure to inform the members that the club had again been favoured with a fairly success- ful season. The weather was very wet at the commence- ment and close of the season, and it might seem para- doxical but it was nevertheless true, that they did not have either an official opening or closing run this season. During the months of May, June, July and August, the weather with few exceptions was almost perfect, and their many runs together were carried out tender brilliant skies which would well compare with the Sunny Sauth. The oecuing rue should have been to Acton Briage on Saturday, March 30th, but owing to the wet on that day, and several of the succe Iding Saturdays, it was net until April 20th, that the Club get going, and then a most pleasant after- noon was spent at the pretty little riverside village of Hale. Mr Pickavance proceeded to mention in detail a number of the enjoyable runs which took place during the season. On Saturday, May 4th, e bowling match between the Captainer and Sub-captain'a teams was played off at Acton Bridge. After a been contest the Captain's team had to submit to a defeat by one point. , On Saturday June Ist, an innovation in the shape of a ' ladies' day was tried, the venue being Dela- mere Forest. Owing to the stormy weather only two ladies turned out, attended by an emart of nine members. However a pleasant afternoon was spent in visitieg the Yeomanry camp at Oektnere and it was to be hoped when "another ladiete day was arranged, that the Clerk of the weather would be memorialized to provide better climatic conditions. On Tuesday June 18th the popular bowling main was com- menced at 800 Green.about 40 members being present. There were 32 entries and after being co atinuecl the week alter at Winvrick, the main was finally concluded at Hoe Green, the winners being J nodmore (let). G Smith (2nd), T J Lee (3rd) and F Baxter' (4th). The main seemed to te tome more popu ar each year and there was no doubt that one or two more during the season might prove beneficial. On Saturday, July 6th, the club was again most hospitably entertained by the worthy President (Mr J Naylor) and his most amiable good lady at their charming residence, Beeston Tower. Magnificent weather prevailed and members and lady friends to the nunifficr of 83 assembled at that pictur- esque spot. One of tee most enjoyable afternoons in the history of the club was spent. On Setuaday August 10th, the annual fishing match took place in the canal at Norton and the winners proved to be J Podmore (let) J Waywell (2ed), and W Brown (3rd). On August 17ch the old time fixture of President's Day was revived, Chester being selected as the destinatioc. The weather in the early part of the afternoon was extremely wet but twenty-five members including six ladies, braved the elements and had a good time. The final Tuesday night run and smoker took place, at Winwick on September 24th. Other runs almost too numerous to mention had been greatly a jayed. They could recall a delightful series of pleasant rune among fair unexpected nooks of nature ; of exhilarating ening over the brown rolling moorland to Outten Park where the golden gorse and purple heather grew in such rich profusion ; of sweet, indelent loiter- ings through the lanes of Arley and Butiworth, with the air laden with the scent of wild roses and honeysuckle ; of pleasant strolls through the leafy avenues of grant' old Dalamere Forest, and dreamy sails up the winding reaches of the Dee at Chester,—an unbroken series of pleasurable wanderings wlech could well compare with any other season. The holiday tours this season bad been very successful and many merry parties had spent pleasant times together. The committee were again approached with the idea of gating up another parade, but after much careful consideration it was decided to leave it over until another year. Personally, the Secre- tary thought it would be a wise thing for the club to favour the project in the ensuing season,.as there was no doubt whatever that the last parade did an immense amount of geed to the cf üb. The attendance at the club , runs this season had averaged 15 for Tuesday nights and 12 for Saturdays, which although not quite so large as in some former years, was still ' much better than most cycling clubs could at present boast of. The attendance prizes had been won by 11 Whittle, and J Newton for Saturday and Tuesday runs combined and F Barber for Tuesday niaffit runs only. The social side of the season had again been moat successful. The billiard handicap which finished early in the year resulted as follows :—J Bibby (Iste G H Smith (2ad), F Barber (3rd) and W H Bellain (4th).Four first class smokers had been held during the year. The best thanks of the club undoubtedly were due to those friends who so kindly entertained them during the long winter months and while not wishing to particularly mention individuals, yet he could not refrain from tendering their best thanks to Mr J L Davenport and Mr Frank Booth for their yeoman services during the past season. The club membership now stood at 93 'which they could reckon most satisfactory as it was exactly the same as last year, notwithstanding the fact that several of their members had left the town (linene the past year. The treasurer's balance sheet showed that the club was in a better financial position than it had been for years, having gained between three and four pounds this last year, a fact which must reflect great credit upon the Chancellor of their Exchequer. In conclusion he could safely assert that the club was still meeting with a goodly share of success, and be might hero state with all the emphasis at his command that it was a piece of sheer nonsense for members to talk of the club being ardyiag concern or a sinking ship. As long as half a dozen of the good old crowd existed, there would be a Warrington Cycling Club, and it the members generally would take a more active interest in all that appertained to the successful working and wen-being of the club, instead of leaving everything to the officials, they seould have a club second to none in the country, and an example to the whole cycling community. They had the members and they had the talent to do the work, therefore let them nail the good old motto to the mast, never to be lowered, namely "sociability, good fellowship, and prosperity for the Warrington Cycling Club." (Applause.) Mr D. DAVIES moved the adoption of the report. He said they had had many reports from Mr Pickavance in the past and he hoped they would be fortunate enough to have many more in the future. A distinction had been conferred upon the Secretary and upon the club by the appointment of Mr Pickavanca as chairman of the Liverpool centre of the N.C.U. Mr Pickavance thoroughly deserved the honour. Mr R. DAINTITH seconded, and the report was unani- mously approved. THE FINANCIAL POSITION. In the absence of the treasurer (Mr A Mounfield through indisposition, the financial statement was sub nutted by Mr Frank Booth (financial secretary). It- appears that the income for the year amounted to £25 19s 6d, and the expenditure to £2l 2s 41, leaving a credit balance of £4 17s 21 There was a balance in the bank from January 1901 of £6, so that the club had now a total balance in hand of £lO 17s 2d. Mr PtexevAtace proposed the adoption of the state- merit and said it showed a very satisfactory state of affairs. It was the first time for many years that the balance amounted to over £lO. Mr SAMPSON seconded and the resolution was agreed to THANKS. Mr W LITTON proposed a vote of thanks to the secl's• tary,financial searetary,and treasurer. He said-the club had a very energetic set of officials and he did not think they could be equalled by any club in the Nor:h of England. Mr TAYLOR seconded and the vote was unanimously accorded. Ms sos BOOTII and PICICAVANCE briefly responded. Mr J L DAVENPORT in prosing a vote of thanks to the Captain (Mr D Davies), sub-captain (Mr J Newton) and Comnaitcee, said they had done their work admir- ably and were entitled to the thanks of the club. In seconding Mr PICKAVANCE said the Committee and officials had worked togetuer most harmenieUely throughout the season. The motion was carried unanimously and Messrs D Davies and W H &Allan responded. Miss KIERNAN was heartily thanked for allowing the club the tree use of the rooms at the Patten Arms Hotel. ELECTION OF OFFICERS, The renowioß Officers Were eleOted : President, Mr John Naylor ; vice-presidents, the Mayor (Mr J C Parr). Messrs R Pierpoint, M.P., W B Roberts, W Pierptiat. T F Kiernan, Ernest Eloughton, C H Wood, T J Huise, D IDavies, W Brown, W U Bellian, Dr Kisby, 3 Critchleee T Mather, J L Davenport, J Newton, J Pod more, and V. Litton ; captain, ma J Sampson ; sub-captain, Mr W ITaylor ; lion treasurer, Mr W Mounfield ; hen secretary Mr E Pickavance NC U. delegates,; financial veretary, Mr Frank Booth; Mr E Pickavance and Mr W H Bellian ; committee, Messrs W 11 Bellian, G H Stn'th, W Litton, J L Davenport, W Brown W Kishy and II Clare ; auditors, Messrs Garnett and Give. THE PROPOSED PARADE. At the close of the meeting Mr D DAVIES sugeeated to the committee that a parade should be held during the season in aid of the Infirmary and Nursing, Associa- tion. They all knew how successful their eff•rl's were on Ixthalf of the Infirmary and he was quite certain that no member of the club would work more heartily than he would, if it was decided to entertain a similar pro- ject ti's year. Mr PICKAVANCE also expressed the hope that a par- ade would be held, • A vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the proceedings.

At the Borough Police Court on Monday morning, before Mr F Monks and other magistrates, Mr Stanley Wilson, deputy town clerk, said the magis- trates bad appointed the following day for the hear- ing, under the Private Streets Works Act, of objec- tions to the final apportionment ot the cost of paving certain streets. Since the court was fixed the heavy downfall of snow had prevented the Corporation witnesses making their examination of the passages and streets. He, therefore, agred for an adjournment of the court to the 25th inst. Mr Longton, on behalf of the objectors, said his witnesses had the same diffiuulties to meet as those of tha Corporation, and they were quite ready to go on with the case. He was in the court now accidentally and was surprised to bear the application.—Mr Wilson said be gave Mr Longtoa notice of the application on the previous Tuesday He should not have made the application now if Mr Longton had not been in court.—The Deputy Mayor (Alderman Roberts) said that Mr Longton I had all his evidence before he made the original I application. The Corporation hal since had to I obtain rebutting evidence.—Mr Longton : That is I so to a certain extent.—The Deputy Mayor said it I was so to the full eor.ent. He knew everything about the case.—Mr Longron eventually agreed to an adjournment to the 25th inst., and this was arranged.

div.head: LATCH FORD BAPTIST CHURCH JUBILEE.
div.p: LATCH FORD BAPTIST CHURCH JUBILEE.

A jubilee tea and reunion were held on Thursiay last week, fee was served in the schoolroom, the tables being presided over by the lady members of the con- gregation. About 120 persons sat down to tea. The subsequent proceedings were held in the church, when there was an encouraging attendance. The Rev J F Matthews, the pastor of the church, conducted the pro- ceedings and he was accompanied on the rostrum by the Rev J W Varley,: of St Annes (formerly pastor of the church), Rev J S Hughes (Hill Cliff e Baptist Church), Mr Wells and Mr John Wilkinson. The choir was in attendance and led the singing and also sang the anthem " What are these." Mr William Wilkinson pre- sided at the organ. In the course of a few introductory remarks, the Pastor referred to the absence termed:l indisposition of Mr Wilkinson, of Antrobter, who was the secior member of the church and brother of the first pastor ; Mr Joseph Albinson, one of the oldest officers; Councillor James Evans, who was an old scholar of the Barn Ceapel school formerly connected with the Church, and the Rev John Yonge, who was suffering from rheumatism. The object of the gathering, he said, was to cover as interestingly as pos- sible the history of their church life at Latchfercl. They had all sides; of their church history represented. In celebration of their jubilee they were hoping to build three new class rooms to meet the urizent demand for further accommodation in connection with the Sunday school. They knew to what an enormous extent their Sunday school had grown, and as the future success of the church very largely depended on the cultivation of Hie young life and cherishing these boys and girls, it was necessary that sotnething should be done ,to provide further accommodation for the grow- ing needs: of the school. They also intended, if possible, to have a pipe organ in the clew*. Between £5O and £7O were stiii in hand from the proceeds of the bazaar held three years ago to meet the expenses in conneetion with the repair and renovation of the church and Mr. Joseph Albinson had promised £5O as a dona- tion to the Jubilee fund for the provision of an organ. He (Mr. Matthews) thought if tiles could raise another £l5O they would wry adequately and joyously celebrate their jubilee. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Matthews then called upon the secretary (Mr. William Thomas Wilkinson), Ito read a repott giving a history of the church and in , doing so paid a tribute to the services of Mr Wilkinson. ' Mr W T WILMNSON in the course of a brie! historical , sketch, stated hint about the year 1849 a number of the members connected with Hill Cliffs Baptist Chapel thought it desirable to withdraw from that communion and for about eighteen months they met together for the worship of God in the private house of one of their number at Stockton Heath. The service; were held in ' the house until it became too small. In 1850 it beceme known to them that the small chapel keewn as the Bars Chapel held by the Wesleyans would be at liberty and it was decided to take it on rental. Toe opening services were held on the 12th January, 1851 ween Mr Oemeron, of Blackburn, preached two sermons. A little later a Sunday school was cornit enced in connection with it. The baptistry in connection with the chapel was at Ackers pits and he (Mr Wilkinson). could remember seeing crowds of people assembling for the purpose of witnessing the ueiqiee spectacle. On to 4th of February it was decided to form the community into a Baptist Church. Mr Joseph Wilkinson was appointed pastor, and Mr Yarwood and Mr Asbbrook, the deacons. The number of members who formed the church was 33 and of that number only 2 survived, Mr and Mrs Wilkieson, of Antrobus, who intended to he present at that meeting if tee weather had been favourable. In connection with the Sunday S ohool, they had one of the first scholars pre- sent that evertine in the Demon of Mrs Grounds who attended it in 1851. In 1359 or 1850 it was thought advisable to build a new chapel and the present site was selected as the most coevenient. Tee Present chapel was opened en March 29th, 1861,and in 1858,the Sunday School was added. The first pastor.Mr Joseph Wilkins on continued to labour there until his death in April 1381, he having pr 'ached the Word of Life for 32 years. Sob- sequently the Rev J W Varley became pastor and remained until October 1894, when he departed for St. Aunts. He: was succeeded by the Rev Charles Andrew who laboured there until his death in 1896. In the following year the Rev J F Matthews accepted the cell to the pastorate and the members hoped he would continue as pastor as long as his services were for the glory of God and the spread of His kingdom. (Hear, hear.) The number of scholars when the school com- menced was nine and at the present time there were 190 scholars and 16 teacheer. The membership of the chnrch had increased from 33 to 103. (Applause). Mr Wilkinson proceeded to read a j Miler) greeleiva from the Rev Joseph Edison. pa ttor of the Baptist Church at Willows, California, who was formerly a scholar at the Sunday school. Mr. WELLS ttrn gave some interesting reminiecencee of the school which be first entered in September 1855. He spoke in appreciative terms of the services of the four pastors who had served the church and asked how many churches could say they had only four pastors in 50 years. The Rev J W VARLEY said it was with peculiar pleasure that he addressed that Jubilee meeting. His thoughts were naturally taken back, not only to his own experience there as a pastor, but to . their experience as a Christian church during the past fifty years. When he was in South Africa be noticed mounds of stones in different places and when he asked the meaning of them he was told that they had been placed there by Kaffirs as signs of their thankful- ness for passing throuele some perilous pei led in their history. He did not mean them to conclude that the '5O years' experience of that church had been perilous times, but they were fifty stones witnessing to God's presence and Gel's faithfulness and goodness. He had often wondered at the audacity of the people connected with that church for inviting him, whilst still a student at Manchester, to become their pastor. He looked back with peculiar feelings of gratification at their display of faith in asking him to become the pastor two years before it was possible for him t.) come. He had always believed in the Latchford people, When a man preached to them he had a people who listened and who were hungering for the grace of God. He had not the privilege of knowing his predecessor but if it , had not been for the foundation work of Mr Wilkinson, the church could not have progressed as it had done. He was abeolut els certain that there had always bcoh a need for a Nenconformist conscience and a Nonconfor- mist church in that district. Whatever might have heen the character and the motive of the clergy of the Eatab- lishrd Church there hid been the necessity for a place of wcrehip for those who believed in a free church, in free institutions and that religious freedom which was the very breath and atmosphere of the New Testament. (Hear, hear). The speaker proceeded to refer to some of the members coenectTid with the church and in con- clusion urged his hearers to be faithful to their Christ- ian profession and they would see still greater progress than that which they now witnessed. (Applause). Mr JOHN WILKINSON also spoke a few encouraging wcrds. The proceedings terminated with the pronouncing o the Benediction by the Rev. J. W. Varley.

CANON KNOX-LITTLE ON "SOCIAL
PURITY,"

The Roy Canon Knox-Little. of Worcester,addressod a large congregation of men at the Parish Church, War- rington, on Friday evening on CU) subject of" Social Purity." Taking for his text the words " Look unto the rock whence ye arc hewn and to the hole of the pit whence ye are digged ; look unto Abra- ham that begat you and unto Safari that bear you," the preacte ti gave an eloquent and powerful dlemurse. He said he was privileged by the great kindness of the Rector of that church to have the opportunity, which was always to him a delightful opportunity.of speaking to Lancashire men, upon a great subj,et. Hi had to speak to thorn on the question of social purity which touched the hearts of all real men, and was the mosi difficult, the most solemn, the most searching qu-isti,n that it was possible for them to think ot. After expounding the text the pr ‘acher went on to say that social purity depended upon the duty of man governing himself. Woat was the difference between the man who allowed his lusts to prevail and the man who did not ? The man who allowed his :usts to pre- vail permitted hill passions to take the throne of his being aod to trample upon himself , and the man who governed himself was the man who made his will the lordly faculty, who made his will supreme and who said to his passions and his wishes and his various desires " Thus far shalt thou go and no farther." Men were divided into two classes, the men who governed themselves by their lordly will and the men who allowed the wild rebellion of passion to govern them. It was like all the political arenas of the world. It wa. like the strong Giivernment, or the weak, sentimental, half •hearted "Iv Government. Tte half-hearted,silly Government allowed things to go anyhow, the strong Government kept things in their proper places. Prc- ceeding, the preacher said that many a lad would be saved from impurity if he had some good man ta speak out to. Many a fellow was drifting into sin because he had no one to speak cut to, whom he could trust in these awful mysteries of life Con- tinuing,he asked his hearers if they as brave Englishmen as hard-headed north countrymen, couli loAar to think of women being degraded and lost through men who were strong enough to save them if the men would only govern themselves. He appealed to them to think of the greatness of he family life that had ben loved by the Anpjc-Salcou race. In conclusion he asked them to live so that in the last great day, no one either man or woman woull be able to (IMO tip and Fay " Morally, lam the worse for him." Let them re - member that right was a great vital principle, that igh, pure, moral principle led to I noble life and a stal- h art faith. •

div.head: WARRINGTON POETESS.
div.p: A WARRINGTON POETESS.
Interesting Paper by Mr. H. Stuart Page.

- . Another of the series of " club-nights " in connec- tion with the Warrington Society, was held at the Old Academy on Thursday last week, when Mr. H. Stuart Page read an interesting paper entitled "A Warrington Poetess."—Mr. C. Madeley presided, and considering be inclemency of the weather, the attendance ot mem' bers was satisfactory. Mr. Pees, at the outset, said the poetess to whom the title of his paper referred was Anna Letitia Aikin, better known to the world as Mrs. Barbauld. To the present generation the name might not convey much meaning, but a century ago it was a household world, levee and reverenced throughout the length and breadth of the land In the course of a brief sketch of the life of Mrs Barbauld, Mr Page said that her mother, a woman of sense and refine- ment, and a gentlewoman, brought her daughter up with that Puritan vigour which was characteristic of the old families to one of which she belonged, who were the pillars of dissent in religious matters and of liberalism in political and intellectual matters. Their strong faith was the family heritage of generations. of suffering and endeavour. They might regret this educa- tional and hereditary influence in the case of Mrs Bar- bauld, because it was probably detrimental to the full development of her poetic talente. Her genius was, undoubtedly of the highest order, but I engaged on emblems which were common to the uni- versal heart of human nature, it often seemed to fall short of the fleal accomplishment of perfect art. 00 had been asked "If Mrs Barbeuld was the poetess you , claim her to be, why are her writings so little known to day ?" Because we to day were out of sympathy with the themes that inspired her When Mrs Barbauld wrote, her writings were devoured from one end of the country to the other. But now the dust of oblivion was fast settling on them and they were being consigned to that limbo of forgotten things that had also swallowed up the themes that Inspired them It was ever so. There were poets whose works the human race would never let die. These were they whose:lyres seemed Fo he strung with the very heart strings of humanity, to whom the mysteries of universal nature, of ky, and sorrow,of human love and hatred, of matter and spirit, of life and death, of time and eternity, unfolded themselves in song. These were the world's singers, of whom Shakes- peare was chief " who sang , not for an age but for all time." These held the mirrcrs up to nature, so .that everywhere, in every age and clime, men saw and recognized the Likeness. On the other hand we had singers equally inTired, who sung for their age alone, and no other could fully under- stand or appreciate their song. They were nrt less important on Oat, account, however, and as the ultimate result they might confer as much benefit on their race as those whose fame was more permanent. Who would understand or appreciate all Tennyson wrote, a century hence? His influence was already on the wane. Ho wrote for his own generation, and in the spirit of the age, and was now losing his power over those who were out of sympathy with the thoughts and sentiments and aspirations of the fifties and sixties. And so we were out of sympathy with the spirit of the times in which Mrs Barbauld wrote and the themes that in- spired her muse. It was an ago of sentimentality and cultivated mediocrity on the one hand and strenuous effort on the other. Each of these phases was reflected in Mrs Barbauld'e I verse. In poems of pure sentiment or simple pathos she had rarely been surpassed and none excelled her in chanting in verse the high ideals of those forces which were in operation in her age which helped to make England fue and great. In her works they often got a g'impse of that light which afterwards shone witlesuch brilliance through the poetry of the nineteenth centirry and she might be classified as one of the earliest representations of that wonderful school. But the perioi was against her, so were the circumstances of her life, and FO were the influencen of heredity and early training. She had in her the true instinct that would have made a great , poetess, but the full filet of her genius was ' ever restrained by the fetters of a strange and narrow creed, from ptlich Fho ceuld not Inleak away, and only when her subject was on all fours with her religious belief, could she find perfect expression. Mr Page went on to speak of Mrs Barbauld'a fifteen years residence in Warrington and remarked that they were stated to have been. the happi- est as well as the most brilliant of her life. Her poem entitled "The Invitation" in which after she has sung the praises of Warrington, of its flew era and its birds and its trees and its placid river, refers to the building in which they were now assembled,as being the one particular glory of the town,was briefly touched upon. Ravine referred to the other works of the poet- -038 the speaker concluded by saying that she had left her mark on the Merritt:lre of the country. Bound to our town ty ties RO numerous and so strong we were jnrtified claiming her as our own, and among the many famous names that had graced the literary annals of Warrington, we must place her's first, not only in our literary history but in our affections.

div.head: EXAMINER. FRIDAY FEBRUARY 21. 1902
div.p: THE EXAMINER. FRIDAY FEBRUARY 21. 1902
THE CORONER AND HIS WORK.
Dinner to Warrington Jurymen.
The New Coroner's Court at Warrington.

To commemorate the opening of the Coroner's Court at the new Constabulary Buildings in War- rington, Mr S Brighouse, county coroner, enter- tamed the first jury who sat in that Court, to dinner at the Patten Arms Hotel on Monday even- ling. Mr S Brighouse eat at the head of the table and Mr Richard Bailey, the foreman of the jury, occu- pied the vice-chair. There were also present in addition to the jurymen, Mr F A Jones (deputy coroner), Mr J C Bate (coroner for 11 eat Cheshire), Mr Carr (Mr Brighouse's clerk), Mr Talbot (chief constable), Mr T Longdin (borough surveyor), Mr Ballard (clerk of the works of the new police buildings), and Mr Barlow (coroner's officer). After the loyal toasts had been proposed and received with musical honours, Mr. F. J. WHITTLE (one of the jurymen) sub- mitted the toast of the worthy host, Mr. Brighouse. He said they were all exceedingly obliged to him for the very hospitable manner in which he had entertained them that evening, as also for his uniform kindness to them as jurymen. They felt that when they had to appear before him they had to appear before a gentleman who always had the interests of the jury at heart. He had always looked upon Mr Brighouse with the greatest admira- tion, and he believed he endeavoured to do his bast not only for the jury but for the witnesses, and especially for the relatives ot deceased persons. (Hoar, hear, and applause). " The toast was received with musical honcurs, cheers being given both for Mr. and Mrs Brighouse. aria BRIGHOUSE AND HIS DUTIES. INTERESTING STATISTICS The CHAinesAN, in responding, gave some inter- esting particulars respecting his duties. He was very ranch obliged to those present, he said, for the kind manner in which the toast was received, This was the first occasion since the 16th January, 1884, when he was appointed to the important office of coroner for South-West Lancashire, that he had had the pleasure of meeting jurymen in other than an official capacity. They knew that on those occasions he had frequently to say to them : " Gentlemen, I am only here to direct you on points of law. The facts remain with you," &c. (Laughter). The present occasion seemed to be a fitting opportunity to say something with respect to the office he held. The popular opinion in South-West Lancashire respecting the Coroner was that he was a gentleman with very little to do, that his life was an easy one, and that he had a sery good salary for doing nothing. (Laughter.) He should like to disabuse the public mind of that erroneous impression. The office had attached to it most onerous duties which called for a certain de- gree of intelligence and a knowledge of law, and, above all things, of common-sense. And common- sense ought to be the predominating quality ; it was a far greater quality than a knewledge of the law. For the live years ending the year 1900 he had travelled 28,547 miles to carry out the important duties of the office, and that was the mileage on which his salary was calculated,because he was not allowed to reckon for the return journey, and he could safely say that tor the five years he had named he had travelled 30,000 miles in order to carry out his duties. (Applause.) He had held 2,316 in- quests in South-West Lancashire, and there was a very good way to test whether a coroner was doing his duty. He said that because Mr J C Bate was present, and no doubt he would take it all to heart. (Laughter.) Out of the 2,316 inquests there were only 210 verdicts of death from natural causes. Therefore there remained 2,103 inquests where deaths were due to other than natural CiUses,and where it was absolutely necessary an inquest should be held. In addition to that, during that period, there were 2,010 cases in which no inquests were hell ; in other words there were reported to aim 2,010 deaths in which he had to consider the circumstances and came ' to the conclusion that no inquest was necessary. 'these fizures would give thosc present some idea of the vast amount of work 'hat was to les done in connection with the office he held. These figures did not include the returns of deaths from lunatic asylums and workhouses; they might add to all these figures another 1,000 deaths which were reported to him from lunatic asylums and workhouses, where he had also to consider the circum- stances and decide whether an inquegt should be held or R•Dt. These were, he contended, sufficient facts to con- vince anyone that there was an amount of work attached to the office that people were not aware of. (Hear, hear.) First of all, under the Infant Life Protection Acts, 1872 and 1397, no death of a child in any house thec C 3111.9 under the purview of the Acts could be regist,red ualess the circumstances had been reported to the coroner, and he had to give his sanction to toe reristration ; arid under the regulation of Railways Act, 1873, he had to make an accurate return to the Borne Office of all the circum- stances attending the death of a person from injuries on the railway. By the Registration of Births and Deaths Act, 1874, he had to supply the Regiatrar of Deaths all the particulars necessary to register the death, while under the Explosives Act, 1875, he had to give the Government Inspector of Expl-sives full notice of death from explosives. Under the Factory and Workshops Act he had to give the inspector notice and see that he , attended the inquests. Then there was the Cal Mines 1 Regulation A'-t. Ells Majesty's Inspector had to receive the notice to attend as well as the certificated manager, theeniners' agent, and the relatives of the deceased, ' and they were generally all a: clegeers drawn, and he had to try to conciliate all ; while under the Lunacy Act, 1890, every death in an asylum no rn itter from what cause, had to be reported t the'l coroner. Unoer the Quarries Act, 1894, a notice of 1! death had to be given to an inspector, and by the Local Government Order, 1890, the deaths of all lunatics in a workhouse bad to be reported to him (Mr Brighouse), who had to make each year a most careful statistical return to the Home Office of every inquest he had held and the verdict arrived at, with the cause of death, together with other detail that took up a considerable amount of time. The office, he could assure them, was no bed of roses. In additice to that he had to corres- pond with the chief constables, the relatives of the deceased, and the solicitors engaged, and last, but by no means least, he had the eye cf the Press c- ntinually upon him—(laughter)—and every foolish thing that was said or done was flashed over the earth. (Renewed laughter.) The post, he contended, was an onerous one, and, without being egotistical, he could say that any- one who had held it for 18 years without getting into hot water was a smart sort of man. (Hear, hear, and applause). If the inhabitants of South-West Lancashire were eatisfied with the manner in which he tried to conduct the duties of the office, he was also satisfied: (Applause). He quite recognized and admitted that he wee a public servant and was paid out of the rates but he had to render service for the money he received. He did that to the best of his ability, and if he failed he could not help it. (Applause.)

div.head: PROP,SED PELE9ENTATION HY THE JURYMEN.
div.p: PROP,SED PELE9ENTATION HY THE JURYMEN.

Mr Warrrta said the Chief Constable and the jury would be glad if the Coroner would accept from them at a future date a photograph of the jury and Mr Tal- bot Ucfortunatsly, owing to the very severe weather which had been experienced they had not been able to get it ready for prebentation that evening. The CLIAIBUAN : It shall have a prominent place amongst me treasures when I receive it. (Oplause.)

TUE CORONER'S OPINION OF JURYMEN. The next toast was the health of '• The Jury." The chairman said it gave him pleasure to propose the toast of the level-headed jurymen, the gentlemen who gener- ally gave the vordicts he would have given if he had, been in their places. (Laughter). After relating some amusing experiences respecting juries, the coroner said a great deal depended upon a jury, who had to be honourable men and decide the que,tiona which wore before them in an honouratls manner. Whoever form- ulated the oath to the jury was a man of common-sense. The jury had to inquire into all things " eithout fear or favour, affection, or ill will," and to give a true ver- dict. As far as he had had experience of South-West Lancashire, the jury did their duty without fear or favour, affection or He did not think they were actuated by local influences. It had been suggested that inquests should he held without juries.—God forbid that that should ever come to pass. There were coroners and coroners ! Juries were a round peg in s round hole and he contended that the community of South- West Lancashire were indebted to the gentlemen who gave their time and talents to serve in what was very often a very thankless r ffice, the only remuneration for ,their services being thanks. He was very much otliged to the jurymen of South-West Lancashire. (Applause.) Mr BAILEY responded, and said from what he bad seen of them. Warrington juries were always very pleased to meet the Coroner. They admitted they had a duty to perform to their King and country. The pre- sent was about the beat " inquest " they bad yet had. (Laughter.) He did not know whether they would be called upon to sign their names as usuaLbut might the Almighty spare Mr Brighouse to continue the duties for which he was so ably endowed, and might they meet again under many happy circumstances. (Applause.) _ _ _

that a great deal depended upon the intelligence and ability of the police force. If the police were slack, and did not display intelligence, throueh no tacit of the Coroner there might be no inquiry when one ought to be held. It was a duty of the police to take the initial steps,and upon what they said was built the structure. Be had received the most able assistance from the police of South-West Lancashire. At one time he was very much opposed to the formation of a borough and county police force, and thought that a national force would be the best for Eng- and, but subsequent experience had told him that that theory was wrong, and be had only to men- tien tha Warrington police force to show it was wrong, as in practice it would not work out. The police work of Warrington was remarkably well done under the super- intendence and guidance of his friend, the Chief Con- stable. (Applause.) Mr Talbot had abilities that would fit him for a higher position than Warrington. (Ap- plause.) The Chief Constable would be the first in the world to admit that be had under him a good and trustworthy body of servants. (tlear,hear.) Referring to Detective Barlow, the Coroner's Officer, Mr Brighouse said he was in the foremost ranks of coronet's officers. lie was a most ideal officer, who never put them to any inconvenience if be could help it, and only asked them to do their duty consistent with the business that had to be carried on. (Applause.) Fie (the chairman) was ' greatly indebtied to the Chief Constable. Everything was done saith speed and correctness, and if a death took place he received information by telephone or telegraph, and got as soon as possible by railway or post an account of all the circumstances attaching to it. And when he Came to the inquiry he found the wit- nesses ready and everything in apple-pie order, and the evidence taken for him, so that as far as Warrington was concerned everything was a bed of roses. (Applause.) The toast was received with musical honours, three cheers being given for the " Chief," and one for Detec- tive Barlow.

div.head: TUE CIIIEV CONSTABLE'SUEPLY.
div.p: TUE CIIIEV CONSTABLE'SUEPLY.

The CIIIEF CONSTABLE in responding to the toast, re. marked that if the coroner thought as highly of him and his abilities as be (the speaker) thought of Mr Brighouse, he should have every reason to congratulate himself. It was always a pleasure to him to have to do businesswith the Coroner. He was only thinking the other day when that memorable inquest was held from which the present. pleasant occasion had arisen, as he hoard the Coroner going so smoothly over the ground which he (the speaker) had ploughed so heavily himself, what a Splendid detective had been lost to the police service, and that if fate by on 3 of the many turns of her wheel had ordained the Coroner to be, instead of adorning his present exalted position, a police officer, the dream of Conan D oyle would have been realised and they would have had an actual Sherlock Holmes in existence. (Hear, hear and applause). What a fine stipendiary he would have made ! (Hear, hear.) It gave him (the Chief CanEable) the utmost pleasure and the most real satisfaction to do business with a gentleman who understood his side of the.ques- Lion. and also his (the police) side, and he found that R., great desideratum in the person of a coroner. He had never attends I an ir,quost without having learnt something of the method of ioquiry—the shortest, the most direct, and the most honest method also of arriv- ing at the truth of the matter uader investigation. and after 22 year ,' work,that was something to say. (Hear, hear, and applause.) Everything Mr Brighouse had said of the Warrington police staff was deserved. (Hear, hoar.) They were as good a body of men, if not th; best, it had ever been his honour and privilege to com- mand. And that ought to be so because he had never seen a police force better treated by the Town Council. the Watch Comenilee, and the magistrates then was the case at Warrington. Their interest, comfort, and well-being were studied in every reasonable and proper way, and they enjoyed many privileges they did not enjoy many years ago—many privileges which were not common ire police forces in the country, and they did their best to merit and deserve what was done for them. (Hear, hear.) Be should also like to add that he had never known a town where the help and sympathy accorded to the police was so heartfelt, so general, and so spontaneous as it was in Warrington. (Applause.) Whenever a policeman was in difficulties in Warriugton there were always bravo hearts and ready han is ready to help the policeman, even at personal risk and from a sense of duty. He wished to take that opportunity of tendering to the public of Warrington the thanks which he felt for the great kindness they had always on every occasion extended to himself and his staff. (Applause.) In Detective Barlow they had a very able adjutant as coroner's officer. After Detective Barlow had made his inquiries and prepared his report, he (the Chief Con- stable) had very little to suggest, and very little to add. (Applause).
TELE WARRINGTON CMIPDRATION. MR LONGDIN RESPONDS.

In prooosiog the Was; of the Corporation of War- rington, the Coroner coupled with it the name of Mr Longitin, the Borough Surveyor, lie remarked that until recemtly the ouly borough in South-Weft Lancas- hire which had provided him with a coroner's court was Bootle. lie was exceedingly obliged to the Warrington Corporation for the accommodation which had be,en , afforded him by the provision el the new coroner's court for himself and his Whsm the new police buildings were about to be erected, Mr Longdin was ex- tremely kind, and before D. brick was laid the plans were submitted to him, and he should never forget that mark of recognition of his office on the part of the Cor- poration authorities. (Applause). Mr LOSGPIN responded on behalf of the Corporation, and stated that although he was not a rrvinber of it he was a representative of it. He had been nearly a quarter of a century in their service. Daring that time tie bad done as much work as a man could possibly do in a progressive town like Warrington ; for it was a pro- gressive town, lie thought that when a man could hold the position of borough surveyor of a town like this for such a long psriod he might be considered to have done his duty. (Hoar, hear). He loved the town in which he had to work from day to day. It had done well for him, and he had endeavoured to do his best for the rate- payers, as Mr Brighouse had done in the position he held as coroner. It wag (ally right that every public official should do his duty to those by whom he was maid, and that bad been his endeavour from the first. For many years Warrington had been without suitable accommo- dation for coronet's inquiries. Ile believed the new buildings would serve the purpose for which they bad been built for at least 25 or 30 years. It was a grati- fication to him to know that Mr Brighouse was pleased with the court. (Applause).

div.head: OTHER TOASTS.
div.p: OTHER TOASTS.

The CRIEV CONSTAB-L-E-8-u-bm-itTeli. the health of" Th Visitors," and referred to the occasion as being unique in many respect?. He coupled the names of Mr F A Jones (deputy corner) and Mr Bate (coroner for West Cheshire) with the toast. Mr F A JONES responded, pointing out that Mr Brig. house had been his greatest friend. If at times Mr Brighouse gave a vigorous expression to his feelings he could assure them that ho possesed the kindest heart. (Applause.) Mr HATE Said he had an attachment for Warrington for a reason with which they were all familiar. He eongratulated the Coroner upon the erectors of the new court, and he could as sure them that there was nothing so degrading toe. Coroner as to have to hold an inquest in a room ill-fitted for the purpose. Warrington was ts be congratulated upon the fact that it had in i's district the best coroner in England. (Applause.) He was, above al, a courteous officer, and no juryman or witness who ever had to appear before him received anything but courtesy at his hands. It was not only necessary that a Coroner should have legal knowledge but he should have commonsense and Mr Briphouse was possessed of that in a high degree. (Applause.) The toast of "The Press" was pr posed by the Coroner in complimentary terms and it was responded to by Mr J Lawton and Mr F Hogan. The health of Mr Carr, no Coroam's clerk, was next drunk.

Toe CORONER bore his tefitirnonv to Mr Carr' S work and worrh, and spoke of him in very flattering terms. Mr CIRR brief! responded, and observed that Mr Brighouse had al ways treated him well. Hs could say the same of the Warrington jurymen with whom he had come into contact. So long as he held his present posi- tion he hoped he should receive the same kindness at their hands. (Applause.) The speeches were agreeably interspersed by vocal items which were contributed by Mr Ballard, Mr Hedgocock Mr Barlow, and Mr Milan. The Coroner, Deputy Coroner, and Mr Carr were obliged to leave early in order to catch a train and tie,/ received a cheer on their departure. The Chief Constable presided at the subseqoent pro- ceedings, and the remainder of the evening was pleasantly spent with song, speech, and recitation. At 11 p.m. the happy gathering dispersed after having thormsghly enjoyed the h,,spitality which the kind thoughtfulness of the Cononer had rendered memorable and unique.

div.head: ALARMINGF ACCIDENT AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: ALARMINGF ACCIDENT AT EARLESTOWN.
ACCOUNT BOOK MANUFACTURERS,
si

THE WARRINGTON POLICE FORCE COMPLIMENTED In submitting the toast of "The Police Force," coupled with the name of the Chief Cmstable, the Chair- man said the public scarcely appreciated what a large part the police played in an inquiry into the death of a person. When a death took place the police had to do all the arduous work, make a careful inquiry, arid • • boil down "the result of their investiaatioes into an official report with sufficient information to enable the Coroner to say whether or not be ought to hold an inquiry, so

On Tuesday afternoon an accident which might have been attended with terrible results, happened in Wargrave-road under the railway bridge. A Midland Railway lurry loaded with bags of sugar and drawn by two horses was proceeding to War- rington. Near the railway bridge the road dipq rather steeply, being slippery with the snow, the horses to keep their feet went at a good speed down the bill. Somehow or other the wheels of the lurry skidded and coming in contact with the curblstone one of the wheels collapsed and the lurry overturned on to the footpath, pulling the shaft horse over, and injuring it. About three tons of sugar was scattered about the road,but it was fortunate the accident happened when it'did,as five minutes later the roadway was filled with children coming from the Wargrave schools. About half-past eight, two other lurries arrived from War- rington and the wreckage was cleared away in a short space of time.

div.head: PENKETH FARMER'S SAD DEATH.
div.p: A PENKETH FARMER'S SAD DEATH.
The Adjourned Inquest.

The adjourned Inquiry into the circumstances attending the death of John Fisher, Martinscroft Farm, Penketh, aged sixty-nine years, who died from injuries received by being thrown from a trap which came in colliEion with a lurry, driven by George Rigby, near Sankey Board Schools, was held at the Red Lion Inn, Penketb, on Monday, by Mr S Brighouse. Alfred Cooke, the owner and driver of the trap, was represented by Mr Arthur Browne, Warrington, and George Rigby was repre- sented by Mr R W Thomas, St Helens. John Fisher, jun.,was the first witness called and he stated that the deceased was his father and was 69 years of age. He could not say whether Cooke and witness's father started off with the lamp lighted or not. His father had told him that there was no lamp on tee lurry with which they collided.—By Mr Thomas: His brother had not told him where the men called during the day, His brother had been with Cooke part of the day.—By the Coroner ; Ile thought his father would have been better by himself.—By Mr Browns; It was not a dark night, and witness could see as far as from the Red Lion to the Crown and Cushion. There were nasty cobbles in the yard," but Cooke drove out of the ! yard perfectly right. Alfred Coake, Cow-lane, Sankey, said he was a great friend of the deceased and his son James. Ho remem- bered the thy of the accident. He drove the governess car to Fisher's at the Martinscroft Farm. James Fisher the son, asked him to drive him to Orford on business. That was a distance of about five miles, Witness drove through Warrington. They started from Fisher's house about dinner time and went to Orford to Fisher's sister's They afterwards called at the King and Queen Irma Padgate-road, to see the landlord. Witness had two mall whisk ies, and prior to that ha had had a bottle of beer at Fisher's sister's house, They then drove borne to Fisher's house right through Warrington. They got to Mr James Fisher's at a quarter past four. Mrs Fisher got them seine tea. They had noth- ing to drink after leavhg the Kisg and Queen until the ;accidtnt occurred. Witness was at James Fisher's house an hour aad is half. Whin no left the yard it was getting dark and the deceased lent him a lamp. The deceased also-decided to accompany wit- ness home as he wished to see Mrs Cooke who was W. When they got near to the Board School the deceased saw something in front of them and toll witoes3 to pull to the near side. Before he had time to do so the accident oceurre.d with the lurry, He did not see any light on the harry. Mrs Clarke and her daughter cams out of the Board School to them and they were taken in there. The lamp side of the car was broken. The middle of the wheel was entirely taken out, and the hoop was left. The lurry caught the car with the hind wheels. Before they could pull to the near side the accident occurred.— Cross-examined by Mr Thomas, witness said he and the deceased had two glasses: of beer at the Crown and Cushion. He knew aMr Norcatt very well, but he did not see or epeak to bins on the night in question. He did not get excited with him. He had no conversation with him that he knew of. He had known Mr Norcott all his life, and if he had had a conversation with him he should have remembered it.

William Norcott, farmer, Bold, said he did a little cycling for business purposes. On the evening in ques- tion ho was on his bicycle going in the direction of Warrington ; and when about 100 yards past the Chapel House ho overtook Mr Cooke who was driving a governess car on the left hand side of the road. Witness posed him on the right hand side. He was going about eight miles an hour. .Witness had gone about 80 yards when he met the lorry and the horses, He heard the re- mark to the pony "Go on," and the animal seemed to go faster. There was a light on the lorry on the right hand side. Toe lorry was well on its proper side—the driver would be about two feet off the footpath. He was walking. Witness was about 15 or 20 yards off when he heard the crash. He heard the homes in the lorry going along Liverpool-road at a tremendous speed. That was what made him think there were two horses attached to the lorry. He jumped off his bicycle and stopped the pony ; the trap was on its side. Cooke came up and said " This is a bit dusty." Witness replied" Yes,it is." Cooke then said that the lorry had run into him," and witness answered " No, it did not. You ran into the lurry. It is entirely your own fault." They got into an argument about the matter, alter which witness wont away t 9 avoid further discussion. The Coroner : Always flee from wrath. (Laughter.) You have Scriptural authority for what you did.

Witness : He who tuns away lives to fight another day. (Laughter.) , The Coroner: That is another way of putting it. Mr Browne said tnere was no desire on the part of his , client to make the driver of the furry responsible. ' The Coroaer : I can quits understand this accident happening without any biome to any of the drivers at this point of the road. Mr Browne : It has boon spread about that Cooke was drunk, but Mrs James Fisher is here and she will tell you that he was perfectly sober. George Rigby, a carter in the employ of Messrs Holman, Mitchell and Gernpany,of St Helens, examined by Mr Thomas said that on the day in question he had been with a load of lead to Stockton Heath. He started hack about four o'clock and when he reached the Black Horse Inn, at Sankey Bridges, he lighted his lamp and fixed it to the lurry. Several persons in the public-house saw him light it. He had had several driaks during the day, hut he was sober. When he was near to the School House he was on ihe near side of the road about 2 feet from the curb. He had the reins in his hand and was arranging the seat on the front of the harry. He turned round and saw something coming towards him. The conveyance collided with his lurry. Witness's horses went off art a gallop, and he had got nearly a mile on the road before he could steady them, and pull them up. The horses had been in an electric tram car accid- ent about three months ago, at Live:pool, while one of the horses was in the explosion at S: Helens two years ago. Witness did not kcow the result of the accieent to the trap. When he got home he reported the fact of the collision to the watchman. He told him that some one must have been killed or injured.—Mr Browne: He had to drink what would keep him warm. He was sober He could keep en the lurry while the horses were , running away. He did not come back to the spot the same night. He did not go back to the Sunday School House to hear if any one had been hart. Mrs Moores was called into the room anl she was asked if she could recognise anyone in the room who , called at the Sunday School 'balsa on the night of the accident to inquire about it. She looked at the persons oresent but stated that she could not definitely recog- nlso the person who called. A Juryman stated that he was told by someone who was in the Black Horse Inn on the night of the acci- dent that the driver of the lorry was seen to light a lamp. Mrs Eliza Risher, called by Mr Browne. said she was the wife of James Fisher. 0 e the day in question Mr Cooke came to her house at 4.10. He " had had some tree," but when he went out et the. house he was quite sober. Be had no lamp and he was supplied wita one. She sent for one and •it Iviras ".given to him.—B v the Coroner : Neither Cooke nor her husband were exactly sober when they got to hoe house. The Coroner said that to his mind this was about as simple a case as it was possible lota jury to have to decide. He did not see that there was any difficulty in it, and if he had been on a jury be Falwell have been able to make up his mind at once. He did not say the jury were going to say that Cooke and James Fisher were drunk, There was no evidence to that efLct, but even their best friends would not admit that they were Sober. In his opinion the accident had been correctly described by the farmer (Nercott) who was also a cyclist. He (the coroner) did not know what the jury were going to say, but he could never bring his mind to say that the driver from Sr. Helens was the man who caused the accident. He did not know whether Mr Cooke caused it or not, but he would never say that Rigby caused it. He said he had his lamp lit. Although Ceoke might have had some drink he had from four to six to got over it, and he had hie tea in the meantime. He (the coroner) could quite understand the accident without any of them being to vaente The jury wore then left by themselves to consider their verdict, and when the witnesses and ethers lead been again admitted to the room, The Coroner (addressing the foreman) Said :—How do you say John Fisher came by his death ? Toe F iremen : By an accident. The Coroner : What do you say about George Rigby? Do you, say any blame attaches to him ? The Foreman. No blame whatever. The Coroner: What do you say about Alfred Cooke ? Any blame attachiny to him ? The Foreman : We think be might have shown a little more care in going round the curve, and the acci- dent would have Leon avoided. The Coroner : If you will allow me to say so that is the most sensible verdict I have heard for some time, and they are just the words I would have used herself. If Cooke had exercised a little more care in going round the curve probably the accident would have been avoided. I thoroughly agree with the words you make use of. The jury then returned a verdict accordingly.

A Company Promoters' Failure.
Mr. Norbury Williams and Persalts, Limited.
Manchester Bankruptcy Court, Tuesday.

RE HATVLD FORD.—The debtor in this case was further examined by Mr W Cobbett on behalf of credi- tors. Cobbett questioned the debtor as to his connection with a company celled Persalts, Limited. The debcor said that a draft prospectus was issued of the company which he proposed to form, but the syndi- cate could not get seven persons with £lOO each to come into it. 1 Mr Cobbett : Was there no syndicate formed ?—I was understood to be the syndicate. What had Andrew Smith, Ernest A &mmons, Henry W Holder, and S Norbuty Williams, the gentlemen whose names appear on the prospectus as intending directors, to do with it 9—They all had a hand in it— the ordinary business that was done. Were they not the Persalts Syndicate 9—They were equally interested with myself in the profits,.but they refused to handle any of the funds. Toe debtor further stated that out of the £4.00 paid to him in connection with the syndicate he spent all but £163. In answer to Mr Buckley, his solicitor, the debtor said the £lOO which he received from Mr Simmons was not sent at his r, quest. It came to him through the request of a mutual friend. With the £I•00 advanced he had paid something over £2OO in actual cash payments on behalf of the Persalts syndicate, and the balancs was retained because he had had no payment for his services and nothing for out-of pocket expenses. He had to spend something in going round and standing dinners to authorities, &c. The examination was adjourned to the next Courtday the Official Receiver remarking that he would be able, he thought, to dispose of it at that time.
_ 'A COMPANY PROMOTER IN THE BANKRUPTCY

COURT." To the Editor of the Manchester Evening News. Sir,—Paintul and unp!e mut as the matter is, I must ask you to permit me to refer to your rer,acrt of the bank- ruptcy examination tc-day of Mc Harold Ford (in th: ccurse of which my name is given as one of the pro• posed dii eaters of a proposed company), and to explain my position. As a matter of fact.tha bankrupt received from four gentlemen the sum of £4OO for the purpose of defraying the expenses of starting this company. I was nct one of these. My connection with the business arose in this way .—A greatly renected gentleman, a relative of Mr Harold Eard, asked ma to investigat 3 the patents and plant which it was proposed to buy. 1 He himself had done so and was satisfied. I stated .that I must make a very full and careful inquiry before I would take any part its the pro- posed company. My inquiry was both felt, carelul.and prolotagEd. I obtained for Mr Ford the opinions of SOlll9 of the best chemists in both England and Scotland, and hold their reports at this moment. The result of this lengthy inquiry was eminently satisfactory. Acc.';rdin2- ly I agreed to become a director if a company were formed. But, according t your rr port, the bankrupt, referring to the faur gentlemen who had agreed to be- come director 3, said "They were equally interested with ' myself in the profits." Speaking tor myself, this is not trv‘. I believe the F.,entleriam who had handed naoney to the bankrupt(of whom I was not oce)had some arrangement as to a share of the profit.i, I had none. I never received a penny, except for my out-of-pecket expenses. A short time before the pnaparation of the draft prospectus Mr Ford bad stated in the presence of hree gentlemen (of whom I was one) that he had texpended only atout £5O out of the £4OO he had received. The tact was, however, that (as stated by him tc-day) all the money had been expended by him, a Isr.ie portion of it upon objects other than that for which the money had been entrusted to him. After this most distressine revelation nobody will be surprised to hear that we declined to have any further con:section with the proposed company, or t J issue any ; prospectus. I had nothing whatever to do with any syndicate, or with the raising of any part of the £400.1 It was only with the greatest difficulty that I ascer- tained, later, the names of the amounts. My part in the business coneieted exclusively in verifying the facts in relation to the property it was propased to purchase, ITherenever was a business more thoroughly and honestly investigated than this, but the pity of it was that a large part of the mooeys entrusted to the bankrupt had been wrongly applied by him. I regret that my name has been introduced into this transaction' but I ash you to allow me thus to set myself right, and to say that I am content to have been associated in this matter with such well-known and highly honourable men as Messrs Andrew Smith (Glasgow), Ernest A. Simmons, and Henry W. Holder —Yours, &c.. S. NORBURY WILLIAMS. 75, Shakespeare-street. Manchester, Feb. 17, 1902.

div.head: SE QUEL TO A FARM FIRE. _ A Great Sankey Farmer's Action at Liverpool Assizes.
div.p: SE QUEL TO A FARM FIRE. _ A Great Sankey Farmer's Action at Liverpool Assizes.
Singular Case.

A local case, the ciicumstances of which were of a singular character, was commenced at the Liverpool Assizes on Tuesday afternoon before Mr Justice Wills and a special jury, Mr Matthew Pimblett Pownall, Brook Side Farm, Great Siokey, brought an action against Captain Michael Hughes,St. Helens,his landlord, to recover £l,OOO damages and out of pocket expenses for breach of his tenancy agreement, by reason of his alleged negligence in allowing the main walls and timbers of the house at Sankey to be out of repair to such an extent that a fire was caused in February, 1899, which produced, it is alleged, shock to the nervous system of the plaintiff's wife and son. Mr Horridge, K.C., and Mr Rigby Swift (instructed by Messrs Browne and Crompton, of Warrington) appeared for Mae plain- tiff, and Mr Pickford, K C., Mr A G Steel, N.C., and Mr Leslie Scott (instructed by Mr II L Riley, of Sc. Helens) for the defeod int. Mr Horridge, in his opening statement characterized the case as an unfortunate one for Mr Pownall—one of the most serious character—and eaid that if the jury saw their way to say that he (counsel) had made out his case the 'damages must be something sabstantial. The want of repair was such that if his case was correct it caused the house to get on fire. The bedroom in which Mr Pownall's son was sleeping caught fire, and the boy was so suffocated that he was for 20 minutes or half an hour insensible. He had since had St Vitus's dance, and would never , possibly be the same boy again. There was another claim. Unfortunately Pownall's wife, after attending the boy, went out of her mind, and had certain delu- sions with regard to the house being always on fire, and her condition was attributed originally to the fire. But, having anelysed the case as counsel, he did not think he should be right in pressing that claim cm the jury, because as far as he could see it was impossible to say that the woman might not have gone out of her mind apart from the fire. The position of the plaintiff was that his boy Was injured f3r life. The plaintiff was a farmer, and he had for many years occupied the Brook Side Farm, Great Senkay, and Captaiu Hughes was a large landowner and employed a gentleman named Mr Campbell as his agent. The premises were taken under an agreement dated 1392, and the defendant ti (Wert )ok to keep the main walls of the building in repair. It was an old-fashioned house, and ic 1896—four years after tho tenancy began —there was a heavy fall of bricks from the chimney into the room below. The landlord would not be res- ponsible for that unless he was told about it, and one of the chief controversies was whether the agent was told about the matter. Mr Campbell was in the habit of going round to place, and Mr Pownall in the pre- sence of witnesses told him what; had happened and asked him to have the matter attended to. He said, " Captain Hughes is away, and you had better etay till be comes back. In these old buildings, if you once com- mence to meddle with them you put yourself in for a great deal." It was never thought the joists would be exposed. The plaintiff kept pegging away to Mr Camp- bell to have the matter put right, but he kept making excuses. He then promised:the metter should be attended to, and then he said," Captain Hughes has been losing heavily' and I am to keep eXtiensee down as much as! can." On the 6th of February, 1899, a fire had been lighted in one of the downstairs rooms The bricks,if they had not originally all given way, had becorned loose:mod by the original fall and the joists were exposed. The fire got hold of the joists, and tae room above, where the boy was sleeping, was set on fire. The family were aroused and went to the boy's assistance, lie was un- conscious for half an hour and he had to be attended by a doctor. Sucsequently the plaintiff went to Mr Carnpleel again and said that his boy's illness had turned out more serious than he expected, and ha asked what Captain Hughes intended to do about the matter. The agent said "He is going abroad." " I will see him," said Mr Pownall, and to that the agent replied, " If you do, you will get notice to quit." Ca.ntain Hughes went to the war, and he was away over a year, and in 1900 Mr Pownall met him at the; Preecet Ae,ricultural*Show and asked him what h 3 was going to do. He asked if Captain Hughes would pay half if he (plaintiff) would, and the reply of the defendant was "You had better not deal with it now, because, perhaps,you are not out of the wood yet." The matter was left over until 1901, when the defendant was written to by the solicitor,and the answer from the solicitor was not uninstructive, be- cause it was a vie:y elaborate argumentative letter. It stated, amongst other things, that hie client would repudiate the liability, and also that the claim was a very stale one. Counsel referred to some of the items in the elairn, and added that the main claim would be for the pain and suffering, the boy had sustained' Plaintiff gave evidence bearing out this statement in detail, and added that his son was not yet better. Dr Murray's fees tor his son were aneut £37. The lad had been to Southport and the Isle of Man for the benefit of his health, and witness had to engage an extra servant and a young man servant. Tne board and wages cost £ll7. He charged £lOO, as the cost of waiting upon his wife. The extra faun labour came to £B3, and there was extra food for the boy. The extra nourishment was put at £125, making over £lOO altogether for the boy, apart from toe wife. He had mid to drive his son about ic consequence of the orders of the doctor.

- By Mr Bickford Ha denied that the boy had always been delicate, or that ho had ever said he would not have put him to work on the farm. He had spent over £1 a week many times in extra nourishment for the lad. He ((he plaintiff), was not well treated as far as repairs went. Mr Campbell now and again did small repairs without consulting Captain Hughes. He had always bad a lot of trouble to get anytbing done. He was afraid to speak to Captain Hughes about the matter for fear of being punished. Witness had brought tbe present action against the defendant, but jl9 had bad no notice yet. Oa the average he saw the Captain twice a year, sometimes be did not see him above once a year. He c3uld not remember wheth2r in any of his , letters to the Captain he complained that be could not get him to do what he wanted. He din not remember fetching any bricks from Sutton Hall (the residence of Mr Campbell) to repair ' the chimney. There was a new grate put in, but wit- ness paid for the work being done. He did cot remem- ber Mr Campbell writing to him to pay the income tax. Later on witness said he remembered receiving a letter about the matter. wthe a was cross-examined about the fire, and his letter to Mr Campbell about it was read, in which the plaintiff said that if the fire had not been discovered the house would have been burnt down.

Mr Pickford : If you had been at Mr Campbell. for two years to get toe chimney repaired, and you wrote to tell him of a fire in the ehirnuey,why did you not say to him : "I have been asking you to repair the chim- ney for the last two years '7 Plaintiff . I used to tell him about it being smoky when he came.

His Lordship (to plaintiff) : I wish you would attend to the question. It seems natural to mast of us that if you had been complaining for two years and a half that Mr Campbell wouhl not do anythisg,you should mention t be fact that a fire bad happened. Plaintiff : I have told him many times about the chimney personally. I did not consider it requisite to write to him about it.
Mr Pickfnrd Is there a single letter during all the years from 1896 up to now, before your solicitor's letter, in which you say the defendant was to blame fcr the fire ?. Dui you ever write one ?

Plaintiff ; I cannot remember. Further questioned, Mr Pownall said that he remem- bered the Captain coming back from S',,uth Africa. He wrote a litter expressing his regret that he could not at- tend the home-cming as he had to sit up night and day with his eon, but he hopNi "all would have a jolly time of it." At that time he believed his eon's illness was caused by the neglect to do tho repairs. Captain Hughes sent a maw to see witness's wile, but she did nothing to his knowledge. Re and the defendant had always bean friendly. Ile had always found the defend• ant a good landlord. He had once reduced plaintiff's rent. Fla had spent the day at the defendant's residence, but he made no rcqaest to him to undertake certain repairs. By Mr Horridge He had spoken to Mr Campbell about the matter. He had had cartloads of bottles of cod liver oil, food, and things of that kind. (Laughter). To the best of his knowledge he had not had the inside of a chimney repaired by bricks being put in the place from which others had fallen.
The further hearing of the case was then adjourned until Wednesday morning.
WEDNESDAY'S PROCEEDINGS. JUDGMENI FOR THE DEFENDANT.
The hearing of tbe action was resumed in the Nisi Prius Cautt at Liverpool Ass!zA before Mr Justica Wills on_Wednseday.. _

Jesse Piindett Pownall,the (son who had to be accom- modated with a chair in the witoese-box), said he remembered some bricks falling from the F toreroom chiminey,and beard his father tell defendant's agent that it smoked so badly that they could not live in it, and it , must be tbraugh the bricks falling down. Before the 1 date of the fire witness was strong and able to go about all right. After he regained con- seiousness, subsequent to the fire, he suffered from twitching. lie went to school for abont a week or ten days, but he found he could not manage, and had to leave. Indcatiog in a model handed to him, witness said that one of the joists ran into the flue,and the bricks came down from underneath that. Witness had not since been able to work• He suffered with his breathing, °elves, and twitching—he felt as if he was breathing down a drain pipe.—By Mr Pickford He was not weakly and very often away from school in consequence before the fire. Mrs Amy Johnson, formerly in the employ of the : plaintiff, ;deposed to the falling of the bricks and hearing the plaintiff tell defendant's a ;eat about it. She heard the, agent say that the matter bad better lie over until the return from abroad of Captain Hughes, as when a start was made in repairing an old house like that there was no telling when it would stop.
Lavina Day,also previously employed by the plaintiff,, said that the lad Jesse was strong and healthy before the accident, and weak afterwards.

Dr Murray, of Penketh, said that he bed attended the lad from about a fortnight after the fire to the present time. Before the fire he was a growing, itPalthy lad. Owing to the shock of the fire he became afflicted with chorea° spasm—which was St Vitus' Dance—of the diaphragm, as the result of which he tad occasionally difficulty in breathing. Witness thought the lad would get all right again, but it would take time. By Mr Pickford : He did not consider the boy at nervous subject, but rather that he had been pampered. Dr Joseph, of Ward ngton, who said be attended the lad in the latter end of 1900, remarked that the fact of the diaphragm boing ins olved in the chorea male his condition apparently alarming and very distressing. William Walker, architect, of Warrington, put in plans of the premises, and stated tbat one of the jsist s went into the chimney flue, By Mr Pickford : The tall of the bricks, he consi- dered, increased the danger. Thomas Davies, builder, of Warring,tou, was presen when the floor of the house was opened up by order o the coart, and he deposed that the joist went intof the flue. This closod the plaintiffs' case. _

_ Mr Pickford pointed out that before the jury could fad a verdict against the defendant the plaintiff had to prove that there was a want ot repair after notice of the particular repair necessary had been given to the agent, that that want of repair occasioned the fire, which took place 4 years afterwards, and that the firo was the cause of the injuries to the boy. Counsel having commented on what he said was the exorbitant way in whizh the damages had teen put before the jury, said that the defendant's income from his landed property was £3,500 a year, and he had always been in the habit of expending whatever was required in repairs upon all his farms. In fact, he had actually expended 50 per cent of his income from property on the farms. Counsel would be able to show from samples of letters tlaat:paesed between Idefendant's agent and the plaintiff that there was only one occasion when any demur was made with regard to work plaintiff asked to be done,and that was afterwards done out of the estate. No complaint had ever been, made abont the bricks falling out of the storeroom chimney, and counsel submitted that plaintiff had failed to make out his case

Henry Flunter Campbell, of Sutton Hall, St Helens, agent to C,ptiin Hughes, of Shirley Hall, said he had a pretty free hand in regard to making repairs, and only consulted Captain Hughes when large amounts of expenditure;were involved. The plaintiff had never told witness about the bricks falling in the store room, and never made any complaint about that room at all up to the time of the fire. In fact,witness knew nothing of it until the statement of the claim, Witness attended at plaintiff's house after the fire, and no complaint was ever made by Pownall as to the fire having been caused by negligence. It was not true as one witness bad said, that witness, when asked to do some repairs to plaintiff's house, said that they must wait until Captain Hughes Came home from abroad. The plaintiff did say in 1900 that hiswrife and sort wen ill because witness had not:repaired the chimney when he (plaintiff) told him that it was dangerous. Witnesi replied : " What rot ; how can I make the chimney dangerous by not re- pairing ? If it WAS dangerous, why did you put the fire in it ?

Captain Michael Hughes, (the defendant) said that for 14 years he had been in the Life Guards, and in February, 1900, he sailed for South Africa. His rela- tions with the plaintiff had always been most friendly, and when witness was on the ship he received from Powuall a very nice letter wishing him Godspeed and a safe return. A year later witness returned, and fre- quently saw the plaintiff. He commiserated with him on his hard luck in having his wife and son ill,but plaintiff never suggested that he (defendant) was re3ponsible [or it. He was willing to help plaintiff to a certain extent, as he had done on a previous occasion. The plaintiff did not suggest negligence until May, 1901, which was the first occasion he made mention of alleged neglect in regard to repairs. Witness asked why he had put his boy into the supposed dangerous room when there were °tilers, but all plaintiff could say was that it was convenient.
Another witness had been cilled for the defence, but the jury intimated that they were ful'y convinced that' the plaiUiff had no case.
His Lordship, in giving judgrnent for the d2fendatat, with costs, remarked that it he had had to decide he should he of tho gam" opinion,
